Clinical Reference

Immune Thrombocytopenia (ITP)

On this page
Acquired autoimmune isolated thrombocytopenia (platelets <100 ×109/L) with no other cause — caused by IgG autoantibody that both destroys platelets in the spleen and sabotages their production in the marrow. It is a diagnosis of exclusion: no test confirms it.
Platelets <100 ×109/L (IWG 2009) Treat if <30 · observe if ≥30 Severity = bleeding, not the number Look at the smear — always Incidence 2–5 / 100,000
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — a dual-hit disease, not just "the spleen eats platelets"

The classic one-liner — "autoantibodies coat platelets and the spleen destroys them" — is true but only half the story, and the missing half is what the modern drugs target.

Hit #1 — destruction. Loss of self-tolerance produces IgG autoantibodies against platelet surface glycoproteins — chiefly GPIIb/IIIa (the fibrinogen receptor, ~67% of patients) and GPIb/IX (the von Willebrand factor receptor, ~60%). The antibody-coated ("opsonized") platelet traverses the spleen, where macrophages read the Fc tail of the IgG through FcγRI and FcγRIII and phagocytose it. Platelet lifespan collapses from ~10 days to hours.

Hit #2 — underproduction, and this is the part people miss. A healthy marrow can raise platelet output roughly 5-fold. If destruction were the only problem, most patients would simply compensate and never become thrombocytopenic. They don't — for two reasons:

  • The factory is attacked too. Megakaryocytes express the same GPIIb/IIIa and GPIb/IX as platelets, so the autoantibody cannot tell mother from daughter. Antibody plus cytotoxic T cells impair megakaryocyte maturation, migration to the vascular niche, and proplatelet formation. Marrow megakaryocyte numbers are normal or increased — but their output is not.
  • The "make more platelets" signal never gets loud. Thrombopoietin (TPO) is made by the liver at a constant rate — it is not transcriptionally up-regulated when platelets fall. Instead TPO is regulated by receptor-mediated clearance: circulating platelets and megakaryocytes carry c-Mpl (the TPO receptor), which binds and destroys TPO. In ITP, platelets are churned out and destroyed rapidly, so there is always a fresh batch of c-Mpl-bearing surface soaking up TPO. The marrow only ever hears a whisper.
The proof that nails itIn aplastic anaemia (no megakaryocytes → no c-Mpl → nothing clears TPO) TPO levels are sky-high. In ITP, TPO is normal or low despite a platelet count of 10 — a physiologically inappropriate response. ITP patients have measurably lower TPO than aplastic-anaemia patients at the same platelet count. That single fact is the entire rationale for the TPO-receptor agonist drug class. (Emmons 1996; Kuter, PMC2789970)

The third route — the liver, and why splenectomy sometimes fails. Anti-GPIb/IX antibodies recruit neuraminidase-1 to the platelet surface, stripping sialic acid and exposing galactose. The bare galactose is grabbed by the hepatic Ashwell–Morell receptor on hepatocytes — a clearance route that is entirely FcγR-independent. Isolated anti-GPIb/IX antibodies are found in 31% of multirefractory vs 10.5% of non-refractory patients. If a patient fails steroids, IVIG and splenectomy — all of which target the spleen/FcγR axis — their platelets may be dying in the liver, where none of those drugs reach.

The Factory, the Delivery Trucks, and the Overzealous Inspectors.
Platelets are delivery trucks built at a factory (the megakaryocyte) whose job is patching potholes in your blood vessels.
• The autoantibody is a bright orange "DEFECTIVE — IMPOUND ME" sticker the immune system mistakenly slaps on every truck rolling off the line.
• The spleen is a roadside inspection station. Macrophage inspectors scan for that sticker with their Fcγ receptors and crush any truck wearing one. That's why trucks vanish so fast.
• The liver is a second, secret impound lot. Some stickers (anti-GPIb/IX) also scratch the paint (strip sialic acid), and the liver's Ashwell–Morell tow-truck hauls in any scratched truck without ever reading the sticker. That's why demolishing the inspection station doesn't always work.
• The inspectors also raid the factory — the assembly line wears the same surface proteins, so it gets stickered and sabotaged too.
• And the cruel twist: the factory only builds more trucks when it hears a radio signal (TPO), broadcast at constant volume by the liver. Every truck on the road absorbs some signal. Normally, scarce trucks → nobody absorbing → factory hears it loudly and ramps up. But in ITP trucks are built and crushed so fast that there's always a fresh batch soaking up the waves. The factory hears only a whisper — and never ramps up. That is "inappropriately normal TPO."
The dual hit. One antibody, two injuries: accelerated splenic clearance and a sabotaged factory that never gets the signal to compensate. Every ITP drug attacks one of these two arms.
Now every drug in this guide has an address on that map:
  • Steroids / IVIG / anti-D → jam the inspectors' scanners (FcγR blockade ± reduced antibody production). Fast — but the stickers keep coming.
  • Splenectomy → demolish the inspection station — and the office where the sticker-printers work (splenic B cells and plasma cells).
  • Rituximab → shut the sticker-printing shop (deplete CD20+ B cells). Slow — existing antibody must decay.
  • Fostamatinib → cut the wire between the scanner and the inspector's hands (Syk, the kinase immediately downstream of FcγR).
  • Rilzabrutinib → cut that wire and turn the printers down (BTK sits in both the FcγR and B-cell-receptor pathways — without depleting B cells).
  • TPO-RAs → ignore the broken radio and phone the factory directly: "BUILD MORE TRUCKS." They don't stop the crushing — they out-produce it. That is exactly why the count falls again when you stop.
Published mechanism map: corticosteroids act on T-regs, B cells and the macrophage; splenectomy removes both the B-cell/plasma-cell niche and the clearance site; rituximab depletes B cells; fostamatinib and IVIG/anti-D block Fc-dependent clearance (red bar = inhibition); the TPO-RA is the only green arrow — the only agent that stimulates rather than blocks, acting on the megakaryocyte (MK).
Martínez-Carballeira D, Bernardo Á, Caro A, et al. — CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
A marrow megakaryocyte — the platelet factory — with its characteristic multilobated nucleus, shedding new platelets. In ITP these cells are normal or increased in number, which is precisely why a marrow biopsy is not needed to make the diagnosis: the problem is their output and the antibody attacking them, not their absence.
Animalculist — CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
The scene of the crime: the splenic red pulp. This is where platelets die in ITP. Blood squeezes slowly through the cords of Billroth and must pass between the endothelial cells of the sinusoids — a deliberate bottleneck that forces every cell into intimate contact with resident macrophages. In health this is quality control, culling senescent cells. In ITP the macrophages read the IgG on the platelet through their Fcγ receptors and destroy a perfectly good cell. The spleen isn't malfunctioning — it is doing its job with the wrong instructions. This anatomy also explains two things: why splenectomy works (remove the bottleneck), and why the spleen is not enlarged in ITP — destroying platelets is routine work, not a burden that hypertrophies the organ.
NIH NIAID — CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (NIH BioArt 574)
ITP is a syndrome, not a single disease. Different pathological pathways — FcγR clearance, hepatic desialylation, complement, T-cell cytotoxicity, marrow suppression — converge on one common feature: thrombocytopenia. That is why response is unpredictable, why ~15% of genuine ITP patients have no detectable antiplatelet antibody at all, and why sequentially trying mechanistically different agents is rational rather than random.
📑

Definitions & classification — the vocabulary that trips people up

Why the name changed (IWG 2009, Vicenza)

The International Working Group deliberately re-engineered the terminology, and each change carries meaning:

ChangeThe stated reason
"Immune" replaced "idiopathic"To emphasise the immune-mediated mechanism — it is no longer idiopathic; we know what it is.
"Primary" replaced "idiopathic"To indicate the absence of any obvious initiating or underlying cause (vs secondary ITP).
"Purpura" was droppedBecause bleeding symptoms are absent or minimal in a large proportion of cases. Calling it "purpura" describes a minority.
The acronym ITP was keptPurely pragmatic — "widespread and time-honored use," and it keeps the literature searchable.
"Acute" was abolishedBecause it is vague and can only be applied retrospectively — you cannot know at presentation whether a case will be self-limited. Use newly diagnosed instead.

Why the threshold is <100, not <150 ×109/L

A genuinely good piece of evidence-based line-drawing, and worth knowing because it comes up:

ReasonThe evidence
Counts of 100–150 are usually benignIn a prospective cohort of otherwise healthy people with platelets 100–150, the 10-year probability of progressing to a persistent count <100 was only 6.9% (95% CI 4.0–12.0). Labelling them "ITP" would medicalise a mostly benign finding.
The 150 cutoff is Western-normedCounts of 100–150 are frequently found in apparently healthy people in some non-Western populations.
It excludes normal pregnancyThe 100 cutoff avoids capturing most gestational thrombocytopenia — a physiologic phenomenon needing no follow-up.

Phases — and why the calendar drives the treatment plan

PhaseDefinition (IWG 2009)Why it changes what you do
Newly diagnosed<3 months from diagnosisApplies to every case at diagnosis. Steroids ± IVIG territory. Many will simply remit.
Persistent3–12 months from diagnosis"Chances of spontaneous remission are still significant," which is exactly why deferring aggressive options (splenectomy) is worth considering. Second-line drugs start here.
Chronic>12 monthsNow the odds of spontaneous remission are low — splenectomy becomes reasonable to discuss; long-term TPO-RA/other agents.
Severity in ITP is defined by BLEEDING, not by the platelet count. This is the single most-missed definition on rounds. IWG 2009: "Severe ITP: presence of bleeding symptoms at presentation sufficient to mandate treatment, or occurrence of new bleeding symptoms requiring additional therapeutic intervention." Their own worked example is deliberately provocative: a patient with chronic ITP, a platelet count of 2 ×109/L, and just a few petechiae and ecchymoses would NOT be classified as "severe." The number frightens you; the bleeding phenotype is what actually stratifies the patient.

Refractory ITP — a stricter word than people think (IWG 2009, all three required)

  1. Failure to achieve at least R, or loss of R, after splenectomy
  2. Need of treatment to minimise the risk of clinically significant bleeding — on-demand or adjunctive therapy alone does not qualify
  3. Primary ITP confirmed by excluding other supervened causes

The logic: splenectomy has "curative potential in more than 60% of cases, a result not yet achievable with any other available treatment," so the panel held that ITP in adults cannot truly be called refractory before splenectomy is attempted. A non-splenectomised patient failing drugs is therefore not "refractory" — the correct chart language is "chronic ITP unresponsive to [agents]."

A live tension worth knowing. This 2009 splenectomy-anchored definition is increasingly out of step with practice — ASH 2019 now advises deferring splenectomy ≥1 year and prefers TPO-RA/rituximab first, and surgical rates have fallen. Use the strict definition for trials; in the chart, just describe the patient precisely.

Primary vs secondary — and the naming convention

Secondary ITP = "all forms of immune-mediated thrombocytopenia except primary ITP," named as secondary ITP (SLE-associated), secondary ITP (HIV-associated), secondary ITP (drug-induced). Roughly: autoimmune disease ~7–10% of all ITP, lymphoproliferative ~2–5%, HCV ~2%, HIV ~1%, plus CVID. In adults the commonest are CLL, B-cell lymphoma, SLE and CVID.

Two naming traps • Isolated ANA and/or antiphospholipid antibodies do NOT make it "secondary ITP" — not without distinctive clinical manifestations of SLE/APS. A positive ANA alone is common and non-diagnostic.
• H. pylori-associated ITP is a retrospective label — it requires demonstrated complete resolution of the ITP after proven eradication. You cannot claim it up front.
• HIT keeps its own name "because of its unique features" — it is never called secondary ITP.
The distinction is not academic: primary and secondary ITP have different natural histories and distinct treatments. In secondary ITP you treat the driver. And drug-induced ITP often remits quickly once the culprit stops — severe cases may need platelet transfusion alone, rather than the immunomodulation you'd reach for in primary ITP. Treating the wrong one wastes months of steroids.

Presentation & findings — and why

🩺

Symptoms & signs — frequency and the mechanism behind each

Every finding in ITP follows from one fact: platelets do primary haemostasis — they plug the thousands of microscopic capillary leaks you spring every day just by existing. Lose them and those leaks stay open. That produces a very specific bleeding signature:

 Platelet-type bleeding (ITP)Coagulation-factor bleeding (haemophilia, DIC, warfarin)
WhereSuperficial — skin and mucous membranesDeep — joints, muscles, retroperitoneum
What it looks likePetechiae, non-palpable purpura, ecchymoses, epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagiaHaemarthrosis, deep haematoma, delayed rebleeding
Timing after injuryImmediate — the plug never formsDelayed — the plug forms, then dissolves for want of fibrin
CoagsNormal PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogenAbnormal
If your "ITP" patient has a haemarthrosis or a deep muscle bleed, stop and rethink. That is not what a low platelet count does. Likewise, abnormal coagulation studies are not part of ITP — they are the film telling you this is DIC, liver disease, or something else entirely.

Frequency table — and the pathophysiology of each finding

Frequencies below are from the McMaster ITP Registry (n=269 adjudicated, confirmed primary ITP) unless otherwise stated. Numbers vary widely between cohorts because of referral bias — a tertiary registry sees sicker patients than a community clinic — so a second cohort is given where it disagrees.

Finding~FrequencyWhy it happens (pathophysiology)
Fatigue / reduced energy~85%The most under-recognised symptom in ITP and the one patients rank highest. Independent of anaemia — driven by chronic immune activation and circulating inflammatory cytokines, compounded by fear-of-bleeding restriction of activity. I-WISh: 85% reported ITP reduced their energy; 77% reduced exercise capacity; 75% limited in daily tasks. ICR 2019 explicitly flags fatigue as a genuine disease manifestation, not a complaint to wave away.
Any bleeding~85%The complement of the 14.9% who never bleed. Bleeding is the rule, but its severity is what defines the disease — not the count.
Grade 2 ("severe") bleeding at ≥1 site56.5%Of these, 83.6% bled at a non-skin site and 62.5% bled at multiple sites — i.e. when ITP bleeds meaningfully, it rarely confines itself to the skin. (McMaster: 152/269)
Skin or mouth bleeding42.8%The registry's combined cutaneous/oral category (115/269). Capillary leaks in skin and oral mucosa go unplugged. See the individual signs below.
— Petechiaewithin 42.8%Pinpoint (1–2 mm), NON-BLANCHING, non-palpable red macules; densest on dependent areas (ankles, feet) and pressure points, because hydrostatic pressure is highest there. Non-blanching because the blood is extravascular — it has already left the vessel, so pressing cannot displace it. Palpable purpura would mean vasculitis, not ITP.
— Purpura / ecchymoseswithin 42.8%Confluent petechiae (purpura, >3 mm) and larger bruises from trivial or unremembered trauma. Patients characteristically report bruises "appearing from nowhere."
— "Wet purpura" (oral haemorrhagic blisters)within 42.8%Blood blisters on buccal mucosa/tongue/palate. The oral mucosa is thin, mobile and constantly traumatised by chewing, so it bleeds at counts where skin merely bruises. Marks the transition from cutaneous to MUCOSAL bleeding — see the red flag below.
— Epistaxis, gum bleedingwithin 42.8%Kiesselbach's plexus and the gingival margin are thin, richly vascular, and mechanically disturbed daily (nose-blowing, brushing). Prolonged/recurrent epistaxis is often the symptom that finally brings the patient in.
Menorrhagia (menstruating patients)common — not separately quantifiedThe endometrial bed is a large raw surface healing by platelet plug each cycle. Frequently the first and only manifestation, and frequently normalised by patient and doctor alike for years. Ask directly — and treat it: menstrual suppression is a legitimate adjunct.
Gastrointestinal bleeding7.1%(19/269) Usually requires a co-existing mucosal lesion (ulcer, angiodysplasia, varices) that a normal platelet count would have silently patched. GI bleeding in ITP should prompt a hunt for the lesion — the thrombocytopenia unmasked it rather than caused it.
Genitourinary bleeding / haematuria4.1%(11/269) Same logic. ⚠️ Note for later: haematuria is a relative contraindication to tranexamic acid — clot retention can obstruct the ureter or bladder outlet.
Intracranial haemorrhage1.4–2.2%The event that kills. ASH 2019 states 1.4% of adults; the McMaster referral registry found 2.2% (6/269); the Italian prospective cohort found 0%. Spontaneous ICH essentially requires a very low count (<20–30) plus, often, a second hit (hypertension, trauma, antiplatelet drug, vascular malformation).
No bleeding at all (incidental finding on a routine CBC)14.9–16.1%(McMaster 40/269; Italian cohort 16.1%) This is why "purpura" was struck from the name in 2009 — a sixth of patients have never had a purpuric spot. Many are found only because someone ordered an unrelated blood count.
Splenomegalyessentially 0% — a finding that refutes the diagnosisThe spleen destroys platelets in ITP; it does not enlarge doing it. A palpable spleen means you are looking at hypersplenism, portal hypertension, lymphoma or CLL instead. This is one of the highest-yield negative physical findings in medicine.
An honesty note on these numbersThe McMaster registry reports bleeding by site category ("skin or mouth") and does not break out petechiae, epistaxis, gingival bleeding or menorrhagia as separate percentages. Rather than invent per-sign figures, those rows are shown inside their parent category. Where cohorts disagree (ICH 0% vs 2.2%; asymptomatic 14.9% vs 16.1%) both are given — no single number is definitive.
Petechiae of the lower leg — platelet count of 3 ×109/L. Note the distribution: dependent (lowest leg, around the ankle) and densest where hydrostatic pressure is greatest. They are pinpoint, flat and non-blanching — press them and they stay, because the blood is already outside the vessel. If a "petechial" rash blanches, or is raised/palpable, you are looking at something else (vasculitis).
James Heilman, MD — CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
"Wet purpura" — petechiae on the tongue, same patient, platelets of 3. This is the finding that should change your tempo. Blood on a mucosal surface means the bleeding is no longer confined to skin. Traditional teaching treats wet purpura as a harbinger of serious haemorrhage warranting urgent treatment. Honest caveat: this is a well-established clinical convention, not a prospectively validated predictor of ICH.
James Heilman, MD — CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Oral petechiae and purpura on the palate. The mouth is the one mucosal surface you can actually see — which makes a careful oral exam a free window onto whether this patient has mucosal bleeding. Look under the tongue and at the palate on every ITP patient, every day they are admitted.
Mdscottis — CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Purpura. When petechiae become confluent they are called purpura (>3 mm). In ITP purpura is characteristically non-palpable — flat, you cannot feel it with your eyes closed. Palpable purpura is vasculitis (inflamed vessel wall with cellular infiltrate), a completely different disease with a completely different workup.
User:Hektor — CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Wet purpura is the tripwire. Dry purpura (skin only) is common and, on its own, rarely lethal. Wet purpura — blood blisters in the mouth, spontaneous gum bleeding, epistaxis that won't stop — marks the crossing from cutaneous to mucosal bleeding, and mucosal bleeding is the company that visceral and intracranial bleeding keep. It does not mean the patient is about to have an ICH; it means they have earned an urgent count, an urgent plan, and probably IVIG rather than steroids alone.
Macrocytic platelets — and why your patient bleeds less than their count says they should. A macrocytic platelet is one abnormally large enough to approach the size of a red cell. In ITP the circulating platelets are young, because they are destroyed within hours of release and never live long enough to grow old and small. Young platelets are denser in granules and more haemostatically active per platelet than the senescent ones padding out a normal count. Ten ITP platelets do more work than ten platelets from a marrow-failure patient — which is precisely why the count is a surrogate and the bleeding is the endpoint.
Osaretin — CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
The count and the bleeding are only loosely coupled — and that cuts both ways. Most fatal bleeding occurs below 30 ×109/L (IWG 2009), and mucocutaneous bleeding generally begins below 30. Yet plenty of patients sit at 10 for years with nothing but bruises. Why? ITP platelets are young and large, and young platelets are more haemostatically active per platelet than the senescent ones that make up a normal count — so 10 ITP platelets outperform 10 platelets from a marrow-failure patient. This is exactly why severity is defined by bleeding, and why you treat the patient rather than the number.
Bleeding risk climbs with age. IWG 2009: "the bleeding risk and the haemorrhagic fatality rate increase with age." A count of 15 in a 25-year-old and a count of 15 in a 78-year-old with hypertension and a prior GI bleed are not the same clinical problem. Age belongs in the treat-or-observe calculus.
🧪

Lab interpretation — why each value moves, and what fools it

ITP is defined as much by what is normal as by what is abnormal. The whole diagnostic power of the basic panel is in the pattern: one lineage down, everything else untouched.

LabIn ITPWhy it moves (mechanism) · what falsely raises/lowers it
Platelet count↓↓ <100 (often <20)Mechanism: FcγR-mediated splenic clearance + hepatic (Ashwell–Morell) clearance + impaired marrow output. Median nadir 15 ×109/L (IQR 4–48) in the McMaster registry.
⚠️ FALSELY LOW: EDTA-dependent pseudothrombocytopenia (platelet clumping/satellitism) — the analyser counts a clump as one platelet. Always confirm a new low count on a smear before treating. Also: a clotted/underfilled tube, or giant platelets being sized as red cells by an impedance counter.
⚠️ FALSELY HIGH/normalised: counters may include fragments or microcytes as platelets.
MPV / platelet size↑ normal or largePlatelets are destroyed within hours of release, so the circulating pool is young = large. Supports ITP.
⚠️ Trap: giant platelets + Döhle-like leucocyte inclusions = MYH9-related inherited disorder; giant platelets also occur in Bernard–Soulier. Large is reassuring; giant with other clues is not.
HaemoglobinNormalShould be untouched — the antibody targets platelet glycoproteins, not red cells.
If low, explain it: ① blood loss from the bleeding itself (commonest); ② Evans syndrome (ITP + autoimmune haemolytic anaemia → check DAT); ③ a TMA (schistocytes); ④ marrow disease; ⑤ iatrogenic — anti-D-induced intravascular haemolysis.
WBC & differentialNormalMust be normal. Any second cytopenia, blasts, lymphocytosis, monocytosis or dysplasia moves you off ITP and toward MDS, leukaemia, CLL or aplasia.
Reticulocyte countNormalNormal unless there has been significant blood loss. ↑Retics with anaemia = haemolysis or bleeding → think Evans or TMA. Also: retic >3% is a label contraindication to anti-D (marker of pre-existing haemolysis).
PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogenNORMAL — and this is the pointITP is a platelet disease; the coagulation cascade is untouched. You order coags in ITP not to diagnose it but to EXCLUDE DIC (↑PT, ↑aPTT, ↓fibrinogen, ↑D-dimer) and liver disease. An abnormal coag panel means your diagnosis is wrong.
LDH, haptoglobin, indirect bilirubinNormalThe haemolysis screen. ↑LDH + ↓haptoglobin + ↑indirect bili + schistocytes = TMA (TTP/HUS) — a plasma-exchange emergency, not an ITP. These also serve as the baseline before anti-D, whose boxed warning is fatal intravascular haemolysis.
Blood group + Rh(D)—Not diagnostic — therapeutic. Anti-D only works in Rh(D)-POSITIVE patients (it needs D-antigen-bearing red cells as decoys). Also flags the non-O blood groups at higher risk of IVIG-associated haemolysis.
DAT (direct antiglobulin test)NegativeA positive DAT = Evans syndrome (concurrent AIHA) — and is a contraindication to anti-D per the label. Order it before you reach for WinRho.
Quantitative immunoglobulins (IgG/IgA/IgM)NormalScreens for CVID, a treatable and important secondary cause. ⚠️ MUST be drawn BEFORE IVIG — after 2 g/kg of exogenous IgG the result is uninterpretable, possibly for months. Also identifies IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies (anaphylaxis risk with IVIG/anti-D).
HIV / HCV (± HBV) serologyNegativeSecondary ITP: HIV ~1%, HCV ~2%. ITP may be the presenting manifestation of either → test everyone. HBsAg + anti-HBc are mandatory before rituximab (fatal reactivation). Bonus: HIV and HCV screening are independently USPSTF-graded services.
Antiplatelet antibody assayDO NOT ORDERLow sensitivity despite high specificity (ICR 2019) — ~15% of genuine ITP patients have no detectable antibody, and it does not correlate with outcome. A negative result cannot exclude ITP and a positive one cannot confirm it. It changes nothing. Don't send it.
TPO levelInappropriately normal/low — but DO NOT ORDERMechanistically fascinating (it is the entire rationale for TPO-RAs) but not standardised and not clinically available for routine diagnosis. ICR 2019: not recommended.
Bone marrow biopsyNOT routine — normal/↑ megakaryocytes if doneAge alone is NOT an indication — a genuine change from older teaching that everyone >60 needs a marrow. Reserve for: refractory/relapsed disease, failure of first-line therapy, or any atypical feature (second cytopenia, macrocytosis, dysplasia, blasts, splenomegaly, B symptoms). Remember MDS was the single commonest alternative diagnosis in the McMaster registry — keep the threshold low in an older patient with an atypical picture, but do not biopsy reflexively.
Read the panel as a shape, not a list. Isolated thrombocytopenia + large platelets + normal coags + normal haemolysis screen + normal everything else = ITP. Every test above earns its place by excluding a specific killer: coags exclude DIC, the haemolysis screen and smear exclude TTP, the differential and smear exclude leukaemia and MDS, the DAT excludes Evans, quantitative Igs exclude CVID, and serologies exclude HIV/HCV. None of them can confirm ITP — that is what "diagnosis of exclusion" actually means in practice.
🤕

Imaging — there is no scan for ITP, and exactly one scan that saves lives

ITP has no diagnostic imaging. No scan makes, confirms or excludes it. Imaging in ITP does exactly two jobs: find the bleed, and look for the organ findings that mean this is not ITP.

StudyWhen to order it (the trigger/threshold)What you are looking for — and what it changes
Non-contrast head CTSTAT — any new headache, confusion, focal deficit, seizure, persistent vomiting, or unexplained drop in GCS, at ANY platelet count. Also any significant head trauma.Intracranial haemorrhage. This is the one imaging decision in ITP that changes survival. Do not wait for the platelet count, and do not wait for the patient to look worse. A positive scan triggers the entire critical-bleed bundle (ICU tab) — a pathway with ~30% adult mortality when it is a true critical bleed. The threshold to scan should be near-zero: the test is 60 seconds and the miss is fatal.
CT angiography / repeat CTICH confirmed; or expanding haematoma / neurological deteriorationUnderlying vascular lesion (AVM, aneurysm) and haematoma expansion. Remember thrombocytopenia often unmasks a lesion rather than being the sole cause.
Abdominal ultrasound (spleen size)If the spleen is palpable, if the picture is atypical, or before splenectomySplenomegaly — which argues AGAINST primary ITP and toward hypersplenism, portal hypertension, lymphoma or CLL. Pre-splenectomy it also hunts for an accessory spleen (a cause of surgical failure and late relapse). A normal-sized spleen is the expected finding — ITP does not enlarge it.
CT abdomen/pelvisSuspected retroperitoneal or intra-abdominal bleed; unexplained Hgb drop with flank/back pain or haemodynamic changeRetroperitoneal haemorrhage — a critical-site bleed that can hide a litre of blood with a soft abdomen. Also lymphadenopathy → lymphoproliferative disease.
Chest imaging / CTAdenopathy suspected; before immunosuppression as clinically indicatedMediastinal/hilar adenopathy → lymphoma. Not routine.
Cranial ultrasound (NEONATE)Neonate of an ITP mother with a platelet count <50 ×109/L at birth (ICR 2019, Grade C)Neonatal ICH. MRI for confirmation can be done without anaesthesia using the "sleep and swaddle" approach 30–60 min beforehand.
EndoscopyGI bleeding — after the count is supportedThe underlying lesion. ITP rarely bleeds from normal gut; find the ulcer or angiodysplasia the platelets were silently patching.
New headache in a thrombocytopenic patient is an ICH until a CT says otherwise. Not a tension headache. Not a steroid headache. Not dehydration. Not the IVIG (even though IVIG genuinely causes headache and aseptic meningitis — that is a diagnosis you make after the scan, never instead of it). Scan first, explain later.

Diagnosis — by exclusion

🔍

There is no test for ITP. There is only the smear and the exclusion list.

ICR 2019 is blunt about this: "No 'gold standard' test exists to reliably establish the diagnosis." ITP is what is left when everything else that causes isolated thrombocytopenia has been ruled out by history, examination, CBC, and expert review of the peripheral blood film.

A subtle trapResponse to ITP-specific therapy (IVIG, anti-D, steroids) supports the diagnosis but does not exclude secondary ITP — many secondary ITPs respond to IVIG too. "It got better with steroids" is not proof it was primary.
The whole diagnostic algorithm hangs off one cheap test: look at the film. Four glances, four different diseases, four completely different next moves.
Misdiagnosis is common and measured. In the McMaster ITP Registry (n=305 adjudicated), the overall misdiagnosis rate was 15.1%; of 295 patients labelled primary ITP, 12.2% were reclassified. What they actually had: MDS (7), other autoimmune disease (7), congenital/familial thrombocytopenia (4), hypersplenism (3), liver disease (3), pseudothrombocytopenia (2), drug-induced (2), H. pylori (2), APS (1), Bernard–Soulier (1), malignancy (1). The tell: misdiagnosed patients had milder thrombocytopenia (median 43 vs 14 ×109/L). The more borderline the count, the more suspicious you should be that this isn't ITP at all.
🔬

The smear — four things to look for, four diagnoses

1. Large / giant platelets, few in number. This is what ITP looks like. Platelets are being destroyed within hours of release, so the ones you see are young — and young platelets are big. The large purple cell centre-frame is a giant platelet, nearly the size of a red cell. Large platelets are also more haemostatically active, which is part of why ITP patients bleed less than their count predicts.
Ed Uthman, Houston TX — CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
2. Platelet clumps or satellitism → the count is a lie. Here platelets rosette around a neutrophil (platelet satellitism). Both this and clumping are EDTA-dependent in-vitro artefacts caused by antibodies against GPIIb/IIIa epitopes that EDTA chelation unmasks. The analyser reports "thrombocytopenia" that does not exist. Fix: repeat the CBC in a citrate (blue-top) or heparin tube. Prevalence ~0.1–2% of hospitalised patients — you will meet this.
Animalculist — CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
3. Schistocytes → STOP. This is not ITP. Fragmented red cells mean a thrombotic microangiopathy — TTP, HUS or DIC. Look for anaemia, ↑LDH, ↓haptoglobin, ↑retics, ↑indirect bilirubin. TTP is a plasma-exchange emergency; steroids alone are inadequate and delay kills. ITP has no schistocytes, no haemolysis, and normal coagulation studies.
Prof. Osaro Erhabor — CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
The comparator. A normal adult film — uniform red cells, no fragments, no dysplasia, no blasts, platelets present and normal-sized. In ITP everything on this film stays normal except that the platelets are scarce and large. Any other abnormality — blasts, dysplasia, hypersegmented neutrophils, a second cytopenia — is the film telling you to look elsewhere.
Keith Chambers — CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
🎭

The mimic list — what else does isolated thrombocytopenia

CategoryMimicWhat discriminates it
ArtefactPseudothrombocytopeniaEDTA-dependent clumping/satellitism on film. Repeat in citrate or heparin tube. ~0.1–2% of inpatients. Check this before you give a single steroid.
TMATTPSchistocytes, haemolysis (↑LDH, ↓haptoglobin), ↑retics, neuro/renal signs, ADAMTS13 <10%. Needs plasma exchange, not steroids alone.
TMAHUS / atypical HUSSchistocytes + AKI ± diarrhoeal prodrome (STEC).
TMADICAbnormal coags: ↑PT/INR, ↑aPTT, ↓fibrinogen, ↑D-dimer. ITP coags are normal — that contrast is the whole point of checking them.
Immune/drugHITHeparin exposure, onset day 5–10, thrombosis not bleeding, 4T score, anti-PF4. Keeps its own name — never "secondary ITP."
DrugDrug-inducedClassic culprits: quinine, sulfonamides/TMP-SMX, vancomycin, piperacillin, β-lactams, linezolid, rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, gold, abciximab/eptifibatide/tirofiban. Remits fast on withdrawal — and severe cases may need platelet transfusion alone, not immunosuppression.
MarrowMDS — the #1 misdiagnosisDysplasia, macrocytosis, monocytosis, other cytopenias, blasts. This is where a marrow biopsy earns its keep — especially age >60.
MarrowLeukaemia / lymphoma / aplastic anaemiaBlasts, adenopathy, pancytopenia, low retics.
NutritionalB12 / folate deficiencyMacrocytosis, hypersegmented neutrophils, ↑LDH.
SequestrationHypersplenism / cirrhosisSplenomegaly — which is absent in ITP — plus stigmata of liver disease, ↓albumin, ↑INR.
CongenitalInherited thrombocytopenias (MYH9, Bernard–Soulier, Wiskott–Aldrich)Lifelong low counts, family history, giant platelets, Döhle-like leucocyte inclusions (MYH9). Does not respond to immunosuppression — and that non-response is often the clue.
InfectionHIV, HCV, HBV, CMV, EBV, H. pylori, sepsisSerology. ITP may be the presenting manifestation of HIV or HCV — which is exactly why you test everyone.
ImmunodeficiencyCVIDLow quantitative immunoglobulins, recurrent sinopulmonary infection. Check Igs BEFORE giving IVIG — afterwards you cannot interpret them.
AutoimmuneSLE, APS, Evans syndrome, ALPSANA/dsDNA, aPL panel, DAT (positive in Evans = ITP + autoimmune haemolytic anaemia).
LymphoproliferativeCLL, B-cell lymphomaLymphocytosis, adenopathy, flow cytometry.
ObstetricGestational thrombocytopenia, preeclampsia/HELLPSee the pregnancy row in the comorbidity table.
TransfusionPost-transfusion purpuraTransfusion 5–10 days prior.
Findings that argue AGAINST primary ITP — any one of these should stop you: splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, B symptoms or weight loss, bone pain, a second cytopenia, abnormal coagulation studies, schistocytes, dysplasia, blasts, macrocytosis, or a lifelong/familial history of low counts.
🩺 Clinic — outpatient diagnosis, the treat-or-observe decision & chronic therapy
Workup

What to order & when

🧪

ICR 2019 tiers the workup — required, useful, and don't-bother

A. Basic evaluation — required in everyone

History & physicalBleeding history and its tempo; all drugs incl. OTC/quinine/supplements; recent infection/vaccination; family history of low counts (inherited disease); transfusion in last 5–10 days (post-transfusion purpura); autoimmune symptoms; recent heparin (HIT). Exam hunts for what should be absent: spleen, nodes, liver.Required
CBC + differentialConfirm the thrombocytopenia is ISOLATED. Any second cytopenia derails the diagnosis.Required
Reticulocyte countMarrow response; screens for haemolysis/Evans.Required
PERIPHERAL BLOOD SMEARMANDATORY — expert review, every patient, before any treatment. The single highest-yield, cheapest test in ITP and the one that prevents the catastrophic misses (clumps, schistocytes, blasts, dysplasia). See the Diagnosis section.Required
Blood group + Rh(D)Determines anti-D eligibility (must be Rh(D)-positive) and transfusion readiness.Required

B. Tests of potential utility — do these in the right patient

HIV serologyTest everyone. ~1% of ITP is HIV-associated and ITP may be the presenting manifestation of HIV. Treat the HIV first — the count often follows. Also a USPSTF Grade A service in its own right.Everyone
HCV serologyTest everyone. ~2% of ITP. Treat HCV first. Steroids can raise HCV viral load — knowing the status changes your first-line choice. USPSTF Grade B.Everyone
HBV: HBsAg + anti-HBcSecondary cause — and MANDATORY before rituximab. Both markers: anti-HBc catches the resolved/occult carrier who is HBsAg-negative but can still fatally reactivate. Checking HBsAg alone is the classic miss.Before rituximab
Quantitative Ig (IgG/IgA/IgM)Screens for CVID. ⚠️ DRAW BEFORE IVIG — afterwards the result is uninterpretable. Also identifies IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies (anaphylaxis risk).Before IVIG
DAT (direct antiglobulin)Evans syndrome (ITP + AIHA). Required before anti-D — a positive DAT is a label contraindication.Before anti-D
H. pylori testingUrea breath test or stool antigen — NOT serology (serology cannot distinguish current from past infection). "In appropriate geographic areas" (ICR 2019). Eradication can raise the count.Selected
TSH + anti-thyroid antibodiesAssociated autoimmunity; thyroid disease can itself alter counts.Selected
PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogenTo EXCLUDE DIC — they are normal in ITP. An abnormal panel means the diagnosis is wrong.Selected
ANA ± anti-dsDNA; aPL panelIf SLE features, or thrombosis/obstetric history. ⚠️ An isolated positive ANA or aPL does NOT make it "secondary ITP" without clinical manifestations.Selected
Pregnancy testEveryone of childbearing potential — it changes the entire management plan and rules out several teratogens.Selected
B12 / folateIf macrocytosis or hypersegmented neutrophils.Selected
Flow cytometry ± marrowIf lymphoproliferative disease suspected (lymphocytosis, adenopathy).Selected

C. Tests NOT routinely needed — and why

TestWhy not
Bone marrow examination"Not recommended routinely" (ICR 2019) unless treatment-refractory, relapsed, or atypical findings. Age alone is NOT an indication — a real change from the older "everyone over 60 gets a marrow" teaching. It does earn its keep when the picture is atypical, because MDS was the single commonest alternative diagnosis in the McMaster registry.
Antiplatelet antibody assays"Low sensitivity despite high specificity" (ICR 2019); does not correlate with clinical outcomes. ~15% of true ITP patients have no detectable antibody. It cannot rule in or rule out. Don't send it.
TPO levelNot standardised, not routinely available. Conceptually central, clinically useless here.
Bleeding timeObsolete, non-reproducible, and it makes a thrombocytopenic patient bleed. Never.
When DOES the marrow earn its keep? Refractory or relapsed disease · failure to respond to first-line therapy · any atypical feature (second cytopenia, macrocytosis, dysplasia or blasts on film, splenomegaly, constitutional symptoms) · before splenectomy in an atypical case. In children, ICR 2019 advises marrow aspiration/biopsy/cytogenetics at 3–6 months if there has been no spontaneous rise and no response to treatment.
Decide

Treat or observe?

🔢

The central outpatient decision — and the guideline is more confident about not treating

Scenario (adult, newly diagnosed)ASH 2019 recommendationStrength / certainty
Platelet <30 ×109/L, asymptomatic or minor (skin-only) bleeding"suggests corticosteroids rather than management with observation"CONDITIONAL
⊕◯◯◯ very low
Platelet ≥30 ×109/L, asymptomatic or minor bleeding"recommends AGAINST corticosteroids and in favour of management with observation"STRONG
⊕◯◯◯ very low
Notice the asymmetry — this is the highest-yield fact in outpatient ITP. The recommendation to treat below 30 is only CONDITIONAL. The recommendation NOT to treat at ≥30 without bleeding is STRONG — one of very few strong recommendations in the whole guideline, and issued on very low certainty evidence. ASH is more confident that you should withhold steroids than that you should give them. Why? Because the natural history at ≥30 is good and steroids are not benign. The instinct to "fix the number" is the instinct to resist.
The governing principle, verbatim from IWG 2009: the goal of treatment is "to provide a safe platelet count (eg, one that prevents major bleeding) rather than correcting the platelet count to normal levels," and "because of the real and potential toxicity of currently available treatments, a critical concept is to avoid unnecessary treatment of asymptomatic patients with milder degrees of thrombocytopenia." ICR 2019 sets the target as maintaining >20–30 ×109/L at least for symptomatic patients, with minimal toxicity and optimised quality of life. You are not treating a number. You are buying haemostatic safety at the lowest toxicity price you can.

Interactive: the ASH 2019 treat-vs-observe / admit tool

This is not a validated risk score — it is a faithful encoding of ASH 2019 adult Recommendations 1a/1b (treat vs observe) and 2a/2b/2c (admit vs outpatient). It returns the guideline's position, its strength, and the reasoning.

Platelet count
≥30 ×109/L
20–29 ×109/L
<20 ×109/L
Bleeding phenotype
None, or minor skin-only (dry purpura)
Mucosal — wet purpura, epistaxis, menorrhagia
Major / critical-site (ICH, GI, retroperitoneal)
Disease status
Newly diagnosed (<3 months)
Established / known ITP
Observe · Outpatient
Individualise UPWARD (i.e. treat at a higher count than the rule) for: occupation or lifestyle risk (roofer, contact sport, frequent falls), need for antiplatelet/anticoagulant therapy, an upcoming procedure, older age (bleeding fatality rises with age), a known bleeding lesion (ulcer, angiodysplasia), poor access to care, or a patient whose anxiety at a count of 25 is itself disabling. The thresholds are a starting position, not a verdict.
Treat

Therapy — first-line → escalation

💊

The ladder — every rung tied to the step it interrupts

Full dose ladders (start → increments → target/max), monitoring, interactions and alternatives for every agent live in the Drug reference. This is the sequence and the logic.

1
Corticosteroids — first-line for essentially everyone who needs treatment
Prednisone 1 mg/kg/day (max 80 mg) ×2–3 wk then taper — ALL of it ≤6 weeks · OR dexamethasone 40 mg/day ×4 days
▾
Steroids work at several steps at once: they reduce autoantibody production (step 1), down-regulate macrophage FcγR expression and phagocytosis (step 2), damp T-cell activation, restore Tregs, and improve vascular integrity directly. Jam the inspectors' scanners, and quietly turn down the sticker printers. ~85% respond initially — but relapse is the rule, because nothing has fixed the underlying tolerance defect.
DrugStartTitration / courseTarget & maxWhy it worksIf intolerant / alternative
Prednisone / prednisolone1 mg/kg/day PO (max 80 mg)
ASH 2019 range 0.5–2.0 mg/kg/day		Full dose ×2–3 weeks, then taper⛔ TOTAL ≤6 WEEKS incl. taper (ASH 2019 STRONG rec 3). Response 4–14 d; peak 7–28 d↓antibody, ↓macrophage FcγR phagocytosis, ↑vascular integrity, restores TregsSwitch to dexamethasone for speed/fewer total steroid days; IVIG if steroids contraindicated (uncontrolled DM, psychosis, active infection, HCV)
Dexamethasone (pulsed)40 mg/day PO or IV ×4 days
FLAT dose — not weight-based		Repeat up to 3 courses (ICR 2019). IWG 2009-era range: 4–6 courses q14–28 dResponse 2–14 d; peak 4–28 d. Preferred if you value speedSame mechanism, higher potency, far shorter exposureSwitch to prednisone if neuropsychiatric effects of high-dose dex are intolerable, or you need a gentle taper while a 2nd-line agent takes effect
Methylprednisolone IV1 g IV daily ×3 days— (pulse)Critical bleeding only — see ICUSame mechanism, maximal/immediate—
Prednisone or dexamethasone? Wei et al, Blood 2016 (n=192, newly diagnosed) settles it honestly: HD-dexamethasone gave a better response at day 14 (82.1% vs 67.4%, P=0.044) and better CR (50.5% vs 26.8%, P=0.001) — but sustained response at 6 months was identical (40.0% vs 41.2%, P=0.884). Independently reproduced by Mazzucconi, Blood Adv 2024 (initial 93.9% vs 78.6%; final 59.0% vs 60.5%, NS). Dexamethasone buys SPEED, TOLERABILITY and ~4 days of steroid instead of 4+ weeks — not durability. Both land in the same place at 6 months.
The 6-week rule is the one to memorise. ASH 2019 strongly recommends against a prolonged course (>6 weeks including taper). "For the majority of patients, a trial of 6 weeks should determine whether a patient is going to enter remission." If they still need steroids at week 6, they do not need more steroid — they need a second-line agent. Steroid overuse in ITP is a documented, measured, real-world harm. Note ICR 2019 says "taper by 6–8 weeks" — follow ASH's ≤6 weeks: it is newer, GRADE-based, and strong.
Steroid-dependence = NON-response. IWG 2009 is explicit: needing ongoing/repeated steroids for ≥2 months to hold the count ≥30 makes the patient a NONRESPONDER, not a responder on maintenance. Rebadging chronic prednisone as "control" is how patients end up diabetic, osteoporotic and cushingoid with an ITP that was never actually treated.
Starting steroids — what to monitor & co-prescribeASH 2019 good-practice statement: monitor blood pressure, glucose, mood/sleep disturbance, gastric symptoms, glaucoma, myopathy, osteoporosis, and assess health-related quality of life. Co-prescribe: PPI if GI risk factors, calcium + vitamin D and bone protection, consider PJP prophylaxis with prolonged high-dose steroid. Write the stop date on the prescription.
1+
Add IVIG — when you need the count up FAST
1 g/kg ×1–2 consecutive days (or 0.4 g/kg/day ×5) — onset 1–3 days
▾
IVIG works by saturating the macrophage FcγR with a flood of irrelevant IgG so the opsonised platelet drives past the inspection station, plus saturating FcRn — which accelerates catabolism of the pathogenic autoantibody itself — and up-regulating the inhibitory FcγRIIB. 80–90% respond; 10–20% don't.

Add IVIG to steroids when:

  1. Active clinically significant bleeding
  2. You need a rise within 24–72 h — IVIG onset 1–3 d, peak 2–7 d. Steroids take 4–14 days. If you need a count tomorrow, steroids alone will not do it.
  3. Before an urgent procedure/surgery
  4. Steroids are contraindicated — uncontrolled diabetes, active psychosis, serious infection, HCV
  5. Pregnancy, especially near delivery
IVIG is a bridge, not a destination. The effect wanes in ~2–4 weeks because you have not stopped antibody production — you have only blockaded the clearance machinery. It buys time for steroids, a TPO-RA, or rituximab to work. Never discharge a patient whose count is being held up only by IVIG without a plan for what happens when it wears off.
The second dose is often unnecessary — and this is an actual label rule. Gamunex-C states verbatim: "If after administration of the first of two daily 1 g/kg doses, an adequate increase in the platelet count is observed at 24 hours, the second dose of 1 g/kg body weight may be withheld." Check the count at 24 h before reflexively giving the second gram. That is one fewer expensive, thrombogenic, nephrotoxic infusion.
IVIG has a boxed warning: THROMBOSIS, renal dysfunction and acute renal failure. "Thrombosis may occur in the absence of known risk factors." Renal failure is commoner with sucrose-containing products and in patients with pre-existing renal impairment, diabetes, age >65, volume depletion, sepsis, paraproteinaemia. Use the minimum dose and infusion rate practicable and ensure adequate hydration. And remember: ITP itself already carries a thrombotic risk — IVIG adds to it.
2
Anti-D immune globulin — narrow niche, real danger
50 mcg/kg (250 IU/kg) IV if Hgb ≥10 · Rh(D)+ AND non-splenectomised AND DAT− AND not haemolysing · 8-hour monitored observation
▾
Anti-D coats the patient's own Rh(D)-positive red cells, which then act as decoys that saturate splenic macrophage FcγRs — "reticuloendothelial blockade." You deliberately feed the inspectors a truckload of red cells so they are too busy to crush the platelets. Elegant — and it works by inducing a controlled haemolytic anaemia, which is exactly why it can kill.
DOSE DISCREPANCY — read carefully. The commonly taught "50–75 mcg/kg" overshoots the FDA label. ICR 2019 and IWG 2009 cite 50–75 and 75 mcg/kg respectively; the WinRho SDF label specifies an initial 250 IU/kg = 50 mcg/kg (Hgb ≥10) and states "safety and efficacy at doses exceeding 300 IU/kg (60 mcg/kg) has not been established." 75 mcg/kg appears nowhere in the label. Use the label: 50 mcg/kg; do not exceed 60 mcg/kg without explicit haematology direction.
 Hgb ≥10 g/dLHgb 8 to <10 g/dLHgb <8 g/dL
Initial dose250 IU/kg (50 mcg/kg)125–200 IU/kg (25–40 mcg/kg) — reduced"Use alternative treatments"
Subsequent250–300 IU/kg (50–60 mcg/kg)125–200 IU/kg (25–40 mcg/kg)—

Eligibility — ALL must be true: ① Rh(D)-POSITIVE (the mechanism requires D-antigen red cells) · ② NON-splenectomised (the mechanism requires a spleen to blockade — Scaradavou 1997: splenectomised patients had "minimal or no response") · ③ DAT-negative and not haemolysing (label: reticulocytosis >3% or a positive DAT → "alternate therapies must be used").

BOXED WARNING — intravascular haemolysis leading to DEATH. "IVH can lead to clinically compromising anaemia and multi-system organ failure including ARDS… severe anaemia, acute renal insufficiency, renal failure and DIC have also been reported." Mandatory: monitor in a healthcare setting for ≥8 hours; dipstick urinalysis for haematuria/haemoglobinuria at baseline, 2 h, 4 h and before discharge. The 8-hour rule exists because 94% of severe reactions began within 4 hours. If transfusion is needed afterwards, use Rh(D)-NEGATIVE red cells so you don't feed the haemolysis.
Two practical traps: ① WinRho contains 10% maltose → falsely high glucose readings on some glucometers — you may treat a hyperglycaemia that isn't there, or miss a real hypoglycaemia. ② Anti-D is not available in Europe (ICR 2019). Its use has declined sharply and for good reason — but it is fast (1–3 d), cheap and small-volume, given to the right patient.
3
Second-line: TPO-RA > rituximab > splenectomy
For ITP ≥3 months that is steroid-dependent or steroid-unresponsive — ASH 2019 Recs 6–9, all CONDITIONAL
▾
RecASH 2019 statement (verbatim)Practical read
6"suggests either eltrombopag or romiplostim"No preference between the two TPO-RAs. (Avatrombopag wasn't assessed — it post-dated the evidence review.)
7"suggests either splenectomy or a TPO-RA"Considered comparable in efficacy — the guideline is genuinely equipoised here.
8"suggests rituximab rather than splenectomy"Rituximab > splenectomy
9"suggests a TPO-RA rather than rituximab"TPO-RA > rituximab
5"suggests corticosteroids alone rather than rituximab and corticosteroids for initial therapy"Do NOT add rituximab up front.

The resulting hierarchy: TPO-RA > rituximab > splenectomy — all conditional, all on very-low-certainty evidence. Where do the newer agents fit? Fostamatinib (FDA 2018) and avatrombopag for ITP (FDA June 2019) are not addressed by ASH 2019 at all — its evidence review cut off in May 2017. Rilzabrutinib (FDA 29 Aug 2025) post-dates every current guideline. Their placement is practice, not guideline.

Defer splenectomy at least 12 months. ASH 2019 Rec 9 remark, verbatim: "If possible, splenectomy should be delayed for at least 1 year after diagnosis because of the potential for spontaneous remission in the first year." ICR 2019 goes further: ≥12–24 months. The reason is simple and absolute: persistent ITP (3–12 months) still has a significant spontaneous remission rate, and you cannot un-remove a spleen. Splenectomy is the most effective durable therapy we have (~60–70% durable CR) and the only arguably curative one — but it is irreversible and buys lifelong OPSI and thrombosis risk.
Choosing between them in real life:
• Wants to avoid surgery / needs a fast, reversible, reliable answer → TPO-RA (60–90% response). Cost is chronicity — the count falls when you stop (though ~25–40% achieve sustained remission off-treatment with a planned taper).
• Wants a drug-free shot at durable remission, no surgery → rituximab (~60% overall response, but only ~40% at 1 yr and 30% at 5 yr). Slow — 7–56 d to onset, up to 180 d to peak. Never a rescue drug.
• Young, fit, >12 months in, wants this over with → splenectomy (66% durable CR). Vaccinate ≥14 days before.
• Eltrombopag vs avatrombopag vs romiplostim and the full titration ladders → Drug reference.
Sequence rituximab and splenectomy deliberately. Vaccines work poorly during rituximab-induced B-cell depletion. If splenectomy is anywhere on the horizon, vaccinate BEFORE rituximab — otherwise you can end up splenectomising an unvaccinated patient who cannot mount a response. Plan the whole sequence at the first second-line conversation, not at the pre-op visit.
4
Third-line / multirefractory — change the mechanism, not the dose
Fostamatinib · rilzabrutinib · MMF/azathioprine · danazol · dapsone · oseltamivir
▾
The unifying idea, verbatim from the pathogenesis literature: "ITP is a syndrome rather than a unique pathology. Different pathological pathways lead to a common feature — thrombocytopenia." That is precisely why sequentially trying mechanistically different agents is rational rather than random. A patient who failed steroids, IVIG and splenectomy has failed the entire spleen/FcγR axis — so reach for something that isn't on that axis.
  • Fostamatinib — Syk inhibitor, blocks the signal immediately downstream of FcγR. 100 mg BID → 150 mg BID at 1 month if platelets not ≥50; stop at 12 weeks if no benefit. Stable response 18% vs 2% placebo in patients with a median 8.5 years of ITP — modest, but by a mechanism nothing else approved uses.
  • Rilzabrutinib (Wayrilz) — FDA-approved 29 Aug 2025, the first BTK inhibitor for ITP. 400 mg PO BID, fixed — no titration. Dual mechanism: blocks FcγR signalling in macrophages and B-cell receptor signalling, without depleting B cells. ⚠️ AVOID PPIs entirely — a genuine trap when half these patients are on steroids + a PPI.
  • MMF — ICR 2019 prefers MMF over cyclosporine for tolerability. See the FLIGHT trial: adding MMF to first-line steroid cut treatment failure 44% → 22% (HR 0.41) — but patients reported worse physical function and fatigue. ❌ Teratogenic.
  • Azathioprine 2 mg/kg/day — very slow (30–90 d onset, up to 180 d to peak). Check TPMT/NUDT15 first.
  • Danazol 400–800 mg/day — onset 14–90 d. Hepatotoxicity, virilisation. ❌ Teratogenic.
  • Dapsone — steroid-sparing option (ICR 2019). Check G6PD first (haemolysis); also methaemoglobinaemia. Exact ITP dose not verified in ICR/ASH — commonly 75–100 mg daily; treat as practice.
  • Oseltamivir (investigational/off-label) — the mechanistic curiosity that works: a neuraminidase inhibitor that blocks desialylation and therefore the hepatic Ashwell–Morell clearance route. 66.6% response in multirefractory patients — but only COMBINED with a TPO-RA or immunosuppressant, never as monotherapy. This is the drug for the patient whose platelets are dying in the liver, where steroids, IVIG and splenectomy never reached.
  • Vinca alkaloids — rapid (peak 7–9 d) but not for chronic use (neuropathy). Emergency/bridging only.
Before calling anyone "refractory," re-examine the diagnosis. Failure to respond to immunosuppression is itself a diagnostic clue — inherited thrombocytopenias, MDS and pseudothrombocytopenia do not respond to steroids because they were never immune-mediated. The McMaster registry found 12.2% of "primary ITP" was something else. Re-take the history, re-look at the film, and consider the marrow before adding a fourth drug.
Monitor

Follow-up cadence

📈

What to recheck, and when

Honesty firstNo high-quality trial defines the optimal monitoring interval in ITP. What follows is sourced practice plus the label-mandated monitoring, which is firm. Where a figure is expert practice rather than trial-derived, it says so.
SituationCadenceWhy
After any dose change or new drugCBC ~1 week laterCatches both non-response and overshoot before it matters.
Stable on unchanged therapyMonthlyStatPearls-sourced practice: "monitored a week after a dose or drug change, and every month once the patient's condition stabilises."
Any new mucosal bleed or petechial rashCheck immediatelyThe bleeding phenotype — not the calendar — drives the count.
Newly diagnosed, untreated, being observedWeekly at first → monthly → q3–6 months as stability proves itselfExpert practice — no guideline specifies an interval. Stated as practice, not evidence.
EltrombopagLFTs at baseline, q2 weeks during titration, MONTHLY once stableLabel-mandated — boxed warning for hepatotoxicity.
RomiplostimCBC weekly during titration, monthly once stableLabel. Remember the ~14-day lag between a dose change and its full effect — the cause of classic overshoot/undershoot oscillation.
AvatrombopagPlatelets weekly until stable ≥50, then monthly. No LFT requirement.Label — the practical differentiator vs eltrombopag.
FostamatinibBP q2 weeks until stable dose, then monthly; LFTs monthly; CBC monthly until stable ≥50Label. Hypertension in 28% — it is an expected effect to manage, not a surprise.
RilzabrutinibBilirubin + transaminases at baseline and as clinically indicatedLabel. No mandated proactive CBC schedule.
AFTER STOPPING any TPO-RACBC WEEKLY — eltrombopag ≥4 wk · avatrombopag ≥4 wk · romiplostim ≥2 wkRebound thrombocytopenia — the count can dip below the original baseline. Label-mandated. Taper, don't stop abruptly.
On steroidsBP, glucose, mood/sleep at each visit; bone healthASH 2019 good-practice statement.
When to stop waiting — IWG 2009's most useful table. Each agent has a window after which response becomes unlikely: "the second number of days is the time after which a response to this particular agent becomes less likely." Prednisone 4–14 d to onset, 7–28 d to peak — still <30 at day 28 on prednisone? Waiting longer will not help. Rituximab 7–56 d onset / 14–180 d peak — do not declare it failed at week 3. IVIG and anti-D are the only agents that work in 1–3 days.
Comorbidities

How comorbidities change ITP

🔗

The company ITP keeps — each one bends both the diagnosis and the drug choice

ComorbidityHow it interacts with ITPWhat changes in management
HIVCauses secondary ITP (~1%); ITP may be its presenting feature.Treat the HIV first — ART alone often corrects the count. Test everyone. Steroids in uncontrolled HIV add infection risk.
HCVSecondary ITP (~2%); ITP may be its presenting feature.Treat the HCV first. Steroids risk raising viral load → prefer IVIG if you need a fast rise. ⛔ Eltrombopag's boxed warning includes hepatic decompensation in chronic HCV.
HBV (incl. resolved/occult)Silent until you immunosuppress it.⛔ Screen HBsAg AND anti-HBc before rituximab — reactivation causes fulminant hepatitis, hepatic failure and death, and can occur up to 24 months after the last dose. Antiviral prophylaxis + monitoring if positive.
H. pyloriSecondary ITP in appropriate geography; the association is real but inconsistent.Test by urea breath/stool antigen, not serology. Eradicate if positive — counts may rise. Note the label is retrospective: you can only call it "H. pylori-associated" after the ITP resolves with proven eradication.
CVID / immunodeficiencyAn important, treatable secondary cause; recurrent sinopulmonary infection.Check quantitative Igs BEFORE giving IVIG — afterwards you cannot interpret them. Changes the whole plan (IgG replacement; caution with B-cell depletion).
SLE / autoimmune disease~7–10% of all ITP. Distinct natural history and treatment.Treat the driver. ⚠️ An isolated positive ANA does NOT make it secondary ITP without clinical SLE.
Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS)The cruel paradox: thrombocytopenia AND a prothrombotic state simultaneously.Do not assume the low count protects them — they still clot. Weigh TPO-RAs carefully (added thrombotic risk). ICR 2019: for patients needing anticoagulation, a platelet count >50 is generally recommended. ⚠️ Isolated aPL positivity alone ≠ secondary ITP.
CLL / lymphoma~2–5% of ITP; the commonest adult secondary causes alongside SLE and CVID.Lymphocytosis, adenopathy, or an atypical film → flow cytometry. Treating the lymphoproliferative disease treats the ITP.
MDS / myeloid malignancyThe #1 ITP misdiagnosis (7/36 reclassifications in the McMaster registry).⛔ Eltrombopag and romiplostim both carry warnings for increased risk of death and progression of MDS to AML. Getting this wrong is not a harmless error — you may accelerate a leukaemia. Low threshold for marrow in the older, atypical patient.
Chronic liver disease / cirrhosisMimics ITP via hypersplenism + reduced TPO production. Splenomegaly is the tell.⛔ Eltrombopag: reduce start to 25 mg for ANY hepatic impairment — including mild (Child-Pugh A), a frequently missed detail. Rilzabrutinib: AVOID in Child-Pugh B–C. ⚠️ Do not cross-apply avatrombopag's separate chronic-liver-disease pre-procedure regimen to ITP — different dose, different rules.
CKDUraemia adds a qualitative platelet defect on top of the quantitative one — they bleed worse than the count predicts.IVIG boxed warning: renal dysfunction/ARF — use sucrose-free product, minimum rate, hydrate. Rilzabrutinib: avoid in severe renal impairment. Consider DDAVP for uraemic platelet dysfunction.
Diabetes mellitusSteroids will wreck the glycaemia; it is not optional collateral.Prefer pulsed dexamethasone (4 days) or IVIG over 4+ weeks of prednisone. Anticipate insulin. ⚠️ Anti-D's 10% maltose gives falsely high glucometer readings — you can chase a fake hyperglycaemia or miss a real hypo. IVIG's renal warning specifically names diabetes.
Prior thrombosis / cardiovascular diseaseITP itself carries an increased thrombotic risk — independent of treatment. Adults with ITP have 1.3–2.2× higher mortality, driven by cardiovascular disease, infection and bleeding.The hardest problem in ITP: they need the antiplatelet/anticoagulant AND they are bleeding. ICR 2019 targets: ≥30–50 for a single agent, ≥50–70 for dual therapy. Weigh TPO-RA thrombosis risk — but do not withhold a TPO-RA from a bleeding patient out of thrombosis fear; do avoid overshooting the count.
Peptic ulcer / GI diseaseITP unmasks lesions rather than causing GI bleeds de novo.PPI with steroids. GI bleeding in ITP should trigger a hunt for the lesion. ⛔ No NSAIDs, ever.
Osteoporosis / fracture risk / fallsSteroids accelerate bone loss; falls + thrombocytopenia = ICH.Calcium/vitamin D, bone protection, the ≤6-week rule. Fall risk should push you to treat at a HIGHER count than the guideline threshold.
Psychiatric illnessHigh-dose dexamethasone causes real neuropsychiatric toxicity; active psychosis is a steroid contraindication.Prefer IVIG or move early to a TPO-RA. If dex is intolerable neuropsychiatrically, switch to prednisone.
Asplenia (post-splenectomy)Lifelong OPSI risk — rare but 50–70% mortality.Any fever in an asplenic patient is an emergency → immediate 3rd-gen cephalosporin, do not wait for cultures. Vaccination boosters, medical-alert ID, patient education. Also: anti-D does not work post-splenectomy.
PregnancyChanges diagnosis, thresholds, drugs and delivery planning.See Special populations.
DRUGS TO AVOID / USE WITH CAUTION IN ITP
AgentWhy
⛔ Aspirin, clopidogrel, ticagrelor, prasugrelIrreversible/potent platelet inhibition on top of thrombocytopenia. You are disabling the few platelets they have left. Stop them (weigh against the indication — a recent DES is a genuine dilemma needing cardiology input).
⛔ NSAIDs (incl. ketorolac)Platelet inhibition plus GI mucosal injury — both arms of the same catastrophe. ICR 2019 specifically says avoid NSAIDs for postpartum/postoperative analgesia if platelets <70.
⛔ Recombinant factor VIIa (rFVIIa)The 2026 ASH/McMaster emergency guideline advises AGAINST it (thrombosis risk); ICR 2019 also lists it as NOT recommended. It survives in older "in extremis" algorithms — do not reach for it.
⛔ PlasmapheresisICR 2019: NOT recommended in ITP. It is the treatment for TTP — do not confuse the two diseases.
⛔ Heparin (if HIT is possible)New thrombocytopenia on heparin at day 5–10 is HIT until disproven — a prothrombotic disease. Score it (4Ts, below) and stop all heparin, including flushes.
⛔ Culprit drugsQuinine (incl. tonic water), sulfonamides/TMP-SMX, vancomycin, piperacillin/β-lactams, linezolid, rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, gold, GPIIb/IIIa inhibitors (abciximab, eptifibatide, tirofiban). Drug-induced thrombocytopenia remits fast on withdrawal and severe cases may need platelet transfusion alone — not immunosuppression. Stopping the drug is the treatment.
⛔ IM injectionsHaematoma. Use the IV, SC or oral route. (Yes — this includes vaccines: plan them around the count.)
⚠️ Tranexamic acid in haematuriaClot retention → ureteric/bladder-outlet obstruction. Caution or avoid.
⚠️ PPIs with rilzabrutinibAVOID entirely — pH-dependent solubility destroys efficacy. Antacids/H2RAs: give rilzabrutinib ≥2 h before. A very real trap in a patient on steroids + PPI.
⚠️ Polyvalent cations with eltrombopagAntacids, calcium, iron, magnesium, zinc, dairy chelate it. 2 h before / 4 h after. The #1 reason eltrombopag "fails."
⚠️ Live vaccinesNot recommended before/during rituximab or significant immunosuppression.
⚠️ TeratogensMMF, cyclophosphamide, danazol, vinca alkaloids — contraception required; avoid in pregnancy.
Special

Pregnancy & special populations

🫂

Pregnancy — different thresholds, different drugs, a second patient

ITP occurs in ~0.83 per 10,000 pregnancies and "has a variable course, usually worsening as pregnancy progresses" (ICR 2019). The diagnosis is made the same way — by exclusion — but the exclusion list grows.

Is it ITP or gestational thrombocytopenia?

FeatureGestational thrombocytopeniaITP
TimingLATE gestationCan occur ANY time — ITP is the commonest cause of thrombocytopenia EARLY in pregnancy
Frequency~10% of all pregnancies have platelets <150 at deliveryRare
DepthCounts <100 are much less common (1.0%) and <80 are RARE (0.1%)Often much lower; presenting count is typically lower than gestational thrombocytopenia (P=.000)
BleedingNoneSkin/mucous membrane bleeding more frequent
Neonatal effectNONE — the baby's count need not be checked if the diagnosis is secureIgG crosses the placenta → the baby can be thrombocytopenic
After deliveryResolvesPersists
The practical rule from ICR 2019: "Patients with a history suggestive of ITP or those with a platelet count <80 ×109/L should be investigated for possible ITP." Below 80 in pregnancy, stop calling it gestational — only 0.1% of gestational thrombocytopenia gets that low. And remember the physiology: the mean platelet count normally falls ~10% in the second half of pregnancy from haemodilution, increased platelet activation/clearance and sequestration in the placenta.
The pregnancy differential that kills: preeclampsia/HELLP, TTP, acute fatty liver of pregnancy, APS. The smear is mandatory — ICR 2019: examination of the film "is required to rule out the presence of red blood cell fragmentation seen with microangiopathic haemolysis and preeclampsia." Check LFTs, BP, urine protein, coags and LDH on every pregnant thrombocytopenic patient. Do not anchor on ITP.

Platelet targets in pregnancy (ICR 2019, all Grade C unless stated)

SituationTarget platelet countNote
Most of pregnancy, not bleeding20–30 ×109/L is safe"A platelet count between 20 and 30 ×109/L in a nonbleeding patient is safe for most of pregnancy."
Delivery≥50 ×109/L"A platelet count ≥50 ×109/L should be obtained for delivery."
Regional/neuraxial anaesthesia≥70 ×109/L"At a platelet count ≥70 ×109/L, in the absence of other haemostatic abnormalities, regional axial anaesthesia can be safely performed."
On anticoagulation (e.g. APS)>50 ×109/LGenerally recommended for patients receiving anticoagulation (evidence level IV).
⛔ NSAIDs postpartumAvoid if <70 ×109/LIncreased haemorrhagic risk.
The epidural threshold is genuinely contested — know the numbers on both sides. ICR 2019 (haematology): ≥70. The ISTH SSC Delphi consensus recommends 80 for placing or removing a neuraxial catheter absent other haemostatic defects. The SOAP interdisciplinary consensus (2021) concluded the risk of spinal epidural haematoma at ≥70 is "likely to be very low" in gestational thrombocytopenia, ITP and hypertensive disorders. The underlying data: a systematic review of 1524 thrombocytopenic parturients included >500 with counts 70–100 (≈300 having epidural blockade) with zero haematomas — but the estimated potential risk was still 0.2%. Below 70 the data are too thin to define risk. Practical points: a spinal may be safer than an epidural below 70 (smaller needle); TEG/ROTEM cannot be recommended for this decision; the trend matters as much as the value — a falling count warrants closer watching than a low-but-stable one; and this conversation belongs with the obstetric anaesthetist well before the due date, not at 3 cm.

Treating maternal ITP (ICR 2019)

TherapyStatus in pregnancy
Oral corticosteroids✅ First-line (with IVIG). Use prednisone/prednisolone — it is extensively metabolised by placental 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, so little reaches the fetus. ⚠️ Dexamethasone and betamethasone CROSS the placenta (which is exactly why they are chosen for fetal lung maturation) — the wrong tool for treating the mother's ITP.
IVIG✅ First-line. Grade B: provides a "rapid, but often very transient, increase" — use to urgently raise the count for bleeding or for delivery.
IV anti-D⚠️ Grade B (evidence IIb) in Rh(D)-positive non-splenectomised women — "appears well tolerated and effective" per a small pilot, but may cause maternal OR FETAL haemolysis.
Combination therapyPrednisone + IVIG ± IV anti-D for refractory disease. High-dose methylprednisolone + IVIG and/or azathioprine if refractory to oral steroid or IVIG alone.
Rituximab⚠️ Only for very severe cases — causes perinatal and neonatal immunosuppression (B-cell depletion in the newborn) with infection risk requiring monitoring.
TPO-RAs⚠️ "May be considered in LATE pregnancy when other treatments have failed, but published information is limited."
Splenectomy⚠️ Rarely needed; if required, perform in the SECOND trimester.
⛔ ContraindicatedMMF, cyclophosphamide, danazol, vinca alkaloids — teratogenic.

Delivery & the newborn (ICR 2019)

RecommendationDetail
Mode of delivery = OBSTETRIC indications onlyGrade B. "The mode of delivery should be determined by obstetric indications, not by anticipation of the neonatal platelet count." ITP does NOT mandate caesarean section — "the very low risk of ICH in the fetus/neonate has not been shown to be lessened by caesarean section."
⛔ AvoidCordocentesis and fetal scalp blood sampling (Grade C). During labour avoid fetal scalp electrodes, fetal blood sampling, ventouse delivery and rotational forceps.
Predicting the baby's countThe ONLY reliable predictor is whether a PREVIOUS SIBLING was thrombocytopenic (Grade B). The maternal platelet count does NOT predict the neonatal count. Previous splenectomy in the mother raises the risk of neonatal thrombocytopenia even if her own count is normal.
Cord platelet countObtain at delivery or as soon as possible. If <100 → repeat daily until stable. ⚠️ Pseudothrombocytopenia is common in neonates (difficult draws → clotted samples) — confirm before acting.
Platelet <50 at birth→ Cranial ultrasound. MRI for confirmation can be done without anaesthesia ("sleep and swaddle" 30–60 min prior).
Neonatal ICHGive IVIG + limited steroids to maintain platelets >100 for 1 week if possible, then >50 for another week. ⚠️ Platelet transfusion may increase neonatal risk.
Neonatal bleeding or platelets <30Give IVIG (± platelet transfusion).
Severe thrombocytopenia >1 week in a breast-fed infantConsider pausing breastfeeding for a few days to see whether the count rises (antibody can transfer in milk).
Severe neonatal thrombocytopeniaExclude neonatal ALLOimmune thrombocytopenia (NAIT) by parental testing — a different disease with a different treatment.
Neonatal thrombocytopenia in babies of ITP mothers: platelets <100 in roughly 15–50%, <50 in 8–30%, <20 in 1–9%, and ICH in <1%. The nadir is often on day 2–5, not at birth — so a reassuring cord count does not end the story. Keep checking.
👶

Children & older adults — the two ends behave differently

 ChildrenAdults
Natural historyUsually self-limiting — often post-viral, most remit spontaneouslyUsually chronic; spontaneous remission ~10–37% (cohorts disagree widely)
Severe bleeding (ASH 2019)20.2% (95% CI 10.0–32.9)9.5% (95% CI 4.1–17.1)
ICH (ASH 2019)0.1–0.4%1.4%
Default approachOBSERVATION even at low counts if bleeding is skin-only — the disease usually fixes itselfTreat if <30 or bleeding
MarrowICR 2019: aspiration/biopsy/cytogenetics at 3–6 months if no spontaneous rise and no treatment response; consider NGS/targeted sequencingOnly if refractory/atypical
H. pyloriPositivity 20–29% in children with ITP, but eradication benefit is inconsistent and cannot be relied uponEradicate if positive in appropriate geography
The "<1% ICH" figure everyone quotes is a PAEDIATRIC number. ASH 2019 puts adult ICH at 1.4%, and the McMaster referral registry at 2.2%. In adults, use ~1–2%, not "<1%." Quoting the paediatric figure to an adult patient understates their risk roughly two- to five-fold.
Older adults — what changesWhy it matters
Bleeding risk and haemorrhagic fatality rise with age (IWG 2009)The same count is a different disease at 78 than at 28. Individualise the treat/observe threshold upward.
Peak adult incidence is ~age 60; sex ratio evens out (F:M ~1.0 over 50, vs ~1.7 overall)ITP is not just a young woman's disease — that stereotype delays diagnosis in older men.
MDS suspicion rises sharplyThe #1 misdiagnosis. Atypical features + age >60 → marrow. Getting it wrong risks giving a TPO-RA (with its MDS→AML warning) to a myeloid neoplasm.
Comorbidity + polypharmacyMore culprit drugs, more antiplatelets/anticoagulants, more falls, more steroid harm (diabetes, osteoporosis, delirium). Anti-D mortality rose with age — most deaths were in patients >65.
Prevent

USPSTF A/B & prevention

🛡️

Grade A & B services that are ALSO part of the ITP workup

HIV and HCV screening are doubly justified in ITP: you are simultaneously excluding a secondary cause and delivering a graded preventive service. This is one of the few places where the workup and the health-maintenance checklist are the same order.

GradeScreenPopulationDate
AHIVAdolescents and adults aged 15–65; younger/older if increased riskJun 11, 2019
AHIV in pregnancyAll pregnant persons, including those presenting in labour with unknown statusJun 11, 2019
BHepatitis CAdults aged 18–79 (asymptomatic, incl. pregnant persons)Mar 2, 2020
BHepatitis BAdolescents and adults at INCREASED RISK (risk-based, not universal)Dec 15, 2020
AHepatitis B in pregnancyPregnant women2019
USPSTF and CDC diverge on hepatitis B — a real, board-relevant discrepancy. USPSTF still recommends RISK-BASED screening (Grade B, Dec 2020) and explicitly states it is "consistent with the 2014 USPSTF recommendation." CDC (MMWR, 10 Mar 2023) recommends UNIVERSAL screening of ALL adults ≥18 at least once in a lifetime with a triple panel (HBsAg, anti-HBs, total anti-HBc), and says anyone requesting testing should get it without disclosing risk. A common exam and teaching error is to attribute the universal-screening change to USPSTF — it is CDC's. Also note: the HIV recommendation, while still current at Grade A, is on the USPSTF in-progress list — verify before quoting late in 2026.

Vaccination — and the two ITP-specific timing traps

VaccineTiming rule
Pneumococcal (PCV)≥14 DAYS BEFORE elective splenectomy. Per CDC/ACIP: doses given during the 14 days before surgery still count as valid; if not given before, administer as soon as the patient is stable afterwards.
Meningococcal ACWY
Meningococcal B
H. influenzae type b (Hib)
Routine adult vaccines (influenza, COVID-19, etc.)⚠️ Give subcutaneously or plan around the count — IM injections risk haematoma at low platelet counts. ⚠️ Live vaccines are not recommended before/during rituximab.
Trap 1 — vaccinate before rituximab, not after. B-cell depletion abolishes the vaccine response for months. Trap 2 — vaccinate before splenectomy, not after. Both traps collide in the patient you rituximab first and splenectomise later: they end up asplenic and unable to respond to the vaccines that keep them alive. Sequence the whole plan at the first second-line conversation.

Counselling — what the patient must leave clinic knowing

  • Return immediately for: any headache, confusion, visual change or weakness; blood blisters in the mouth; nosebleed that won't stop after 20 min of pressure; black or bloody stool; blood in urine; any head injury — however trivial.
  • No aspirin, no NSAIDs, no ibuprofen — including the OTC cold remedies that hide them. Paracetamol/acetaminophen is the safe analgesic.
  • Avoid contact/collision sport and high-fall-risk activity while the count is low; soft toothbrush; electric razor.
  • Quinine is in tonic water. A genuinely under-taught cause of drug-induced thrombocytopenia.
  • Menorrhagia is treatable — ask about it and offer menstrual suppression rather than accepting it.
  • Fatigue is real, common (~85%), and independent of the count — it is a disease manifestation, not weakness.
  • If splenectomised: fever = emergency, carry a medical-alert ID.
Scores

Calculators

🧪

PLASMIC score — "is this TTP instead?"

This is the single most important calculator on this page. TTP presents as thrombocytopenia and can be mistaken for ITP — but TTP needs plasma exchange within hours, and treating it as ITP with steroids alone can be fatal. If your thrombocytopenic patient has schistocytes, anaemia, a high LDH or any neuro/renal involvement, score them now.
Platelet count <30 ×109/L +1
Haemolysis: retic >2.5%, undetectable haptoglobin, or indirect bilirubin >2.0 mg/dL +1
NO active cancer (treated within past year) +1
NO history of solid-organ or stem-cell transplant +1
MCV <90 fL +1
INR <1.5 +1
Creatinine <2.0 mg/dL +1
0
