Read the score backwards and it teaches you TTP. Four of the seven points are awarded for things being normal or absent — no cancer, no transplant, MCV <90, INR <1.5, creatinine <2.0. Why? Because those findings point away from TTP toward DIC (high INR), marrow disease/B12 deficiency (high MCV) or HUS/renal TMA (high creatinine). TTP is the disease with profound thrombocytopenia and haemolysis but NORMAL coagulation and NORMAL renal function. Which, incidentally, is exactly the trap: normal coags is also what ITP looks like. The discriminator is the haemolysis and the schistocytes.
Bendapudi PK, et al. Lancet Haematol 2017;4(4):e157–e164. Point values verified against MDCalc.
🩸

4Ts score — "is this HIT instead?"

The other can't-miss mimic — and the one where getting it wrong is backwards: HIT is a PROTHROMBOTIC disease. The patient with new thrombocytopenia on heparin does not need platelets; they need every drop of heparin stopped and a non-heparin anticoagulant started. HIT keeps its own name and is never called "secondary ITP."

Thrombocytopenia
>50% fall AND nadir ≥20 +2
30–50% fall OR nadir 10–19 +1
<30% fall OR nadir <10 0
Timing of fall (day 0 = first heparin exposure)
Clear onset days 5–10, or ≤1 day if heparin within last 30 days +2
Days 5–10 but not clear; or onset after day 10; or ≤1 day if heparin 30–100 days ago +1
≤4 days with no recent heparin exposure 0
Thrombosis or other sequelae
New thrombosis, skin necrosis, or acute systemic reaction after IV heparin bolus +2
Progressive/recurrent thrombosis; erythematous skin lesions; suspected but unproven thrombosis +1
None 0
oTher cause for thrombocytopenia
No other explanation +2
Possible other cause evident +1
Definite other cause present 0
8
Note the shape of HIT vs ITP. HIT rarely goes below 20 — a nadir of 5 actually scores zero on the first T, because that is not what HIT does. ITP goes to 5. HIT goes to 60 and throws a clot. If your "HIT" patient has a platelet count of 4 and is covered in petechiae, reconsider.
Lo GK, Juhl D, Warkentin TE, et al. J Thromb Haemost 2006;4(4):759–65. Point values verified against the published criteria table.
🪥

Procedural platelet target — "how high do I need them before this procedure?"

Consensus-based targets from ICR 2019 Table 6, for an adult with ITP at typical bleeding risk. Evidence level IV — consensus, not trial data. The target always bends to the clinical situation, the urgency, and the consequences of bleeding at that particular site.

Dental prophylaxis (descaling, deep cleaning)
Simple dental extraction
Complex dental extraction
Regional dental block
Minor surgery
Major surgery
Major neurosurgery
Starting a single antiplatelet or anticoagulant
Dual antiplatelet, or antiplatelet + anticoagulant
Neuraxial/regional anaesthesia (obstetric)
Delivery
≥20–30
×109/L
Notice how low most of these are. A simple extraction needs only 30; minor surgery 50. The instinct to push everyone to 100 "to be safe" means more IVIG, more steroid and more toxicity for no benefit. Only major neurosurgery demands 100 — because that is the one place where a small bleed is catastrophic.
🔗

Scores we deliberately DON'T reimplement here

An interactive calculator is only as safe as its arithmetic. Where the exact point values or the underlying model cannot be verified from a primary source, this guide links out rather than guesses:

  • ITP-BAT (IWG 2013 bleeding assessment tool) — Rodeghiero et al, Blood 2013;121(14):2596. Grades bleeding across three domains — Skin, visible Mucosae and Organs (SMOG) — scoring the worst manifestation in each. It is a descriptive instrument, not an arithmetic score, and ICR 2019 notes the ITP bleeding tools "have not been validated in large prospective studies," so "a more precise definition of 'clinically relevant' bleeding cannot be given." Read the primary paper.
  • Khellaf bleeding score — the simple score ICR 2019 cites as an example of using bleeding severity to choose steroids alone vs steroids + IVIG. Based on subjective judgement of external bleeding at onset. Exact item weights not verified here.
  • 4Ts on MDCalc — open the validated version for the full reference and probability bands.
  • PLASMIC on MDCalc — open the validated version.
Why this matters more than it looksITP has no validated severity score that decides treatment — and that is not an oversight in this guide, it is the state of the field. IWG 2009 defines "severe" by clinician judgement of bleeding sufficient to mandate treatment, and then concedes the bleeding tools are not prospectively validated. The count is measurable and the bleeding is what matters — and medicine has never fully reconciled the two. Resist the urge to let a number make the decision for you.
Escalate

Red flags → ED / admit

🚑

"Don't manage this in clinic"

Red flagWhy — and what happens next
ANY neurologic symptom — headache, confusion, focal deficit, seizure, vomitingICH until proven otherwise. → ED now, STAT non-contrast head CT, critical-bleed protocol. Do not "watch it overnight."
Any major or visceral bleeding — GI, GU, retroperitoneal, intraocularCritical-bleed pathway → ICU.
"Wet purpura" — oral/mucosal haemorrhagic blistersMarks the crossing from cutaneous to mucosal bleeding → urgent count, urgent treatment, likely admission.
Platelet <20 ×109/L, NEWLY diagnosedASH 2019 Rec 2a suggests hospital admission — the diagnosis is unconfirmed and the trajectory unknown. (An ESTABLISHED patient at the same count who is not bleeding can go home — Rec 2b.)
Epistaxis that won't stop; extensive or rapidly progressive purpuraEscalating bleeding — the trend is the warning, not the absolute count.
Falling haemoglobinOccult bleeding — or haemolysis if anti-D was given.
Fever + thrombocytopeniaConsider sepsis, DIC, TTP. If asplenic: OPSI — treat immediately, do not wait for cultures.
Suspected TTP — schistocytes, haemolysis, neuro/renal signsMedical emergency — plasma exchange, not steroids alone. Score PLASMIC and call haematology from the room.
Need for anti-D administrationRequires ≥8 hours of monitored observation — not deliverable in a standard clinic.
Uncertain diagnosis needing expedited workupExclude TTP/leukaemia fast.
Social/access factors — can't return, lives far, unreliable follow-upA safe count at home requires someone to check it. Disposition is a medical decision.
The one that ends careers and lives: a thrombocytopenic patient calls with a new headache and is told it's probably nothing. ICH is a 1.4–2.2% event in adult ITP with ~30% mortality when critical. The CT costs 60 seconds. Scan.
🛏️ Wards — acute inpatient management
Admit

Who to admit

📋

Admission criteria — and the distinction everyone misses

Scenario (adult)ASH 2019 recommendationStrength
NEWLY DIAGNOSED, platelet <20 ×109/L, asymptomatic or minor bleedingSuggests HOSPITAL ADMISSIONConditional ⊕◯◯◯
ESTABLISHED ITP, platelet <20 ×109/L, asymptomatic or minor bleedingSuggests OUTPATIENT managementConditional ⊕◯◯◯
Platelet ≥20 ×109/L, asymptomatic or minor bleedingSuggests OUTPATIENT managementConditional ⊕◯◯◯
Same count. Opposite disposition. The variable is NEWLY DIAGNOSED vs ESTABLISHED.
A brand-new patient at 12 ×109/L → admit. Why? The diagnosis is unconfirmed (12% of "primary ITP" turns out to be something else), the trajectory is unknown (is this 12 on the way to 3?), and they have never been observed on therapy.
A known ITP patient who has lived at 12 ×109/L for three years and isn't bleeding → home. They have a diagnosis, a known trajectory, a haematologist, and years of evidence that they tolerate this count.
Experience with one's own disease is itself a safety factor. The number on the screen is identical; the clinical situation is not.

Additional admission triggers (synthesised — not from a single graded recommendation)

  • Any clinically relevant bleeding with a low count — this is "severe ITP" by the IWG 2009 definition
  • Wet purpura / mucosal bleeding
  • Any major bleeding → likely ICU, not the floor
  • Need for IVIG or other urgent parenteral therapy not deliverable as an outpatient
  • Anti-D administration — requires ≥8 hours of monitored observation per the boxed warning
  • Uncertain diagnosis needing expedited workup (must exclude TTP/leukaemia now)
  • Social/access factors — unable to return, lives far from care, unreliable follow-up. A safe count at home requires someone to check it.
  • Elderly with comorbidity — bleeding fatality rises with age; ICR 2019 notes the usual 20–30 target "may not be appropriate" for patients >60
Admission is often about the DIAGNOSIS, not the count. The most valuable thing an admission delivers in newly diagnosed ITP is not a drug — it is a haematologist looking at the film, a full secondary-cause screen back within 24 hours, and someone watching the trajectory. You are admitting them to find out what they have.
Orders

Admission order set

🧪

Labs — and the sequence traps

CBC + differentialBaseline; confirm ISOLATED thrombocytopenia.Admit
PERIPHERAL SMEARReviewed by pathologist/haematologist — MANDATORY. Clumps, schistocytes, blasts, dysplasia. Before any treatment.Admit
Citrate-tube platelet countIf ANY clumping on the film → excludes pseudothrombocytopenia. Otherwise you are about to treat a lab artifact with steroids.If clumping
Reticulocyte countMarrow response; screens for Evans/haemolysis; retic >3% contraindicates anti-D.Admit
LDH, haptoglobin, indirect bilirubinHaemolysis screen — EXCLUDE TTP/Evans. Also the baseline before anti-D.Admit
DATEvans syndrome; required before anti-D (positive = contraindication).Admit
PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, D-dimerEXCLUDE DIC. Normal in ITP — abnormal means your diagnosis is wrong.Admit
Type & screen; blood group + Rh(D)Transfusion readiness; determines anti-D eligibility. Add crossmatch if bleeding.Admit
Quantitative immunoglobulinsCVID. ⚠️ DRAW BEFORE IVIG — this is the single most common irreversible sequencing error on the wards.BEFORE IVIG
HIV, HCV, HBV (HBsAg + anti-HBc)Secondary causes; HBV mandatory before rituximab.Admit
CMP incl. creatinine + LFTsBaseline before IVIG (renal — boxed warning) and eltrombopag/fostamatinib (hepatic).Admit
Pregnancy testAll of childbearing potential — changes management entirely.Admit
ANA ± dsDNA, aPL panel; H. pylori; TSHSelected patients (see Clinic workup).Selected
STAT non-contrast head CTAny headache, confusion, focal deficit, seizure or vomiting — at any count.If neuro sx
Two irreversible sequencing errors, both made in the first hour: ① Giving IVIG before drawing quantitative immunoglobulins — you have now made CVID undiagnosable for months. ② Giving steroids before the film is reviewed — if this was TTP, you have delayed plasma exchange; if it was pseudothrombocytopenia, you are treating a tube artifact. The film and the Igs cost nothing and take minutes. Get them first.
📝

Medication reconciliation — the highest-yield intervention on admission

  • HOLD ALL antiplatelet agents — aspirin, clopidogrel, ticagrelor, prasugrel, NSAIDs. (A recent drug-eluting stent is a genuine dilemma — get cardiology involved rather than deciding alone.)
  • HOLD / reverse anticoagulants — warfarin, DOACs, heparin.
  • STOP any potentially culprit drug — quinine (ask about tonic water), sulfonamides/TMP-SMX, vancomycin, β-lactams/piperacillin, linezolid, rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, GPIIb/IIIa inhibitors, heparin (→ think HIT). Drug-induced thrombocytopenia remits fast on withdrawal — stopping the drug IS the treatment.
  • Avoid IM injections — haematoma.
  • Avoid rectal temperatures/suppositories and unnecessary urinary catheters.
  • PPI if starting steroids with GI risk factors. ⚠️ But NOT if you are starting rilzabrutinib — PPIs must be avoided entirely with it.
  • Bowel regimen — avoid straining/Valsalva.
  • Menstrual suppression if menorrhagia (hormonal therapy — an ICR 2019 adjunctive measure; progesterone IUD or OCP).
VTE prophylaxis — an honest answerI could not verify a guideline-specified platelet threshold for VTE prophylaxis specific to ITP. Commonly cited practice is to hold pharmacologic prophylaxis below ~30–50 ×109/L and use mechanical prophylaxis (SCDs), individualising by thrombotic risk. State this as practice, not guideline. Remember the counterintuitive part: ITP patients still get VTE — the disease itself is prothrombotic — so "low platelets" is not blanket permission to skip thromboprophylaxis thinking.

Nursing & supportive orders

  • Fall precautions · soft toothbrush · electric razor only · no contact activity
  • Neuro checks every shift — new headache = STAT head CT, written as a standing order
  • Daily oral exam — look under the tongue and at the palate for wet purpura
  • Document bleeding sites explicitly each shift — severity is defined by bleeding, not the count
Treat

Acute inpatient management

💊

Match the therapy to the urgency — the only question that matters is "how fast do I need this count up?"

SituationTherapyDoseWhy / onset
Needs treatment, not bleeding significantlyCorticosteroid alonePrednisone 1 mg/kg/day (max 80 mg) ×2–3 wk then taper, ALL ≤6 wk total
OR dexamethasone 40 mg/day ×4 days		Onset 4–14 d (pred) / 2–14 d (dex). Neither works overnight.
Bleeding, OR need a rapid rise, OR pre-procedureCorticosteroid + IVIGIVIG 1 g/kg ×1–2 consecutive days (or 0.4 g/kg/day ×5)Onset 1–3 d, peak 2–7 d. ICR 2019: use a combination "in emergency situations in which there is an urgent need to increase the platelet count within 24 hours."
Rh(D)+, non-splenectomised, DAT−, no haemolysis, Hgb ≥10± Anti-D (steroid-sparing / rapid alternative)50 mcg/kg (250 IU/kg) IV over 3–5 minOnset 1–3 d. Requires 8-h monitored observation + dipstick UA at 0/2/4 h and before discharge.
Mucosal / menorrhagic bleeding+ Tranexamic acid (adjunct)15–20 mg/kg every 8 hours (ICR 2019)Antifibrinolytic — stabilises the clot you can form. ⚠️ Caution/avoid in haematuria. No RCT has evaluated TXA specifically in ITP.
Steroids contraindicated (uncontrolled DM, psychosis, active infection, HCV)IVIG first-line insteadAs aboveASH 2019 (HCV-associated secondary ITP): "the initial treatment should be IVIG" (grade 2C).
CRITICAL bleed→ Go to the ICU tab. Different disease, different tempo, different protocol.
PLATELET TRANSFUSION ON THE WARDS — the rule that separates ITP from every other thrombocytopenia.
Do NOT transfuse platelets prophylactically for a low count alone in ITP. Transfused platelets carry the same GPIIb/IIIa and GPIb/IX targets as the patient's own — the autoantibody destroys them within minutes to hours. The increment is minimal and transient, and you have achieved nothing but an alloimmunisation risk.

The contrast that makes it click: in hypoproliferative thrombocytopenia (chemotherapy, marrow failure), prophylactic transfusion at <10 ×109/L is standard — because the marrow is the problem and transfused platelets survive normally. In ITP the marrow is not the problem; the immune system is. You cannot out-transfuse an autoantibody.

The exception — and it is absolute: in active critical bleeding, transfuse. ICR 2019: platelet transfusions "must not be postponed in cases of life-threatening bleeding, especially intracranial haemorrhage." Give them together with IVIG/steroids, often repeated or continuous, and accept that the increment is poor. A poor increment during an ICH is still worth having.
Why steroid + IVIG together beats either alone in the urgent patient: they attack different steps. IVIG blockades the FcγR immediately (onset 1–3 days) but wears off in 2–4 weeks because antibody production never stopped. Steroids are slow (4–14 days) but reduce antibody production and macrophage FcγR expression, so they hold the ground IVIG took. IVIG buys the time; the steroid uses it. Giving IVIG alone and discharging is how patients bounce back at week three.
Monitor

What to trend daily

📈

The daily assessment

ParameterFrequencyWhy
Platelet countDaily (BID if bleeding/critical)The primary endpoint — and the timing tells you whether the agent is working (IWG Table 3 windows).
Bleeding assessment — skin, mucosa, organ; document SITESEVERY SHIFTSeverity is defined by BLEEDING, not the count (IWG 2009). This is the actual endpoint; the platelet count is a surrogate.
Neurologic statusEvery shift + PRNICH is the killer. New headache → STAT CT, no negotiation.
HaemoglobinDailyOccult blood loss — and haemolysis if anti-D was given.
Vital signsPer protocolTachycardia/hypotension → occult haemorrhage.
If on anti-D: urine dipstick (haematuria/haemoglobinuria), LDH, haptoglobin, bilirubin, HgbBaseline, 2 h, 4 h, end of the 8-h windowBoxed warning: fatal intravascular haemolysis. 94% of severe reactions begin within 4 hours.
If on steroids: glucose, BP, mood/sleepDailyASH 2019 good-practice statement.
If on IVIG: creatinine/BUN; watch for thrombosis, headache/aseptic meningitisBaseline + intervalsIVIG boxed warning: thrombosis + renal failure.
The trap of the rising count. A patient whose platelets climb from 8 to 45 on IVIG looks like a success — and they are, for about two weeks. IVIG wears off. If the steroid isn't working underneath it, that count is coming back down at home. Before you celebrate the number, ask what is holding it up and whether that thing will still be there in a fortnight.
Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Escalation triggers — concrete, not "if unstable"

Transfer to ICU for ANY of:
  • Intracranial haemorrhage — confirmed, or suspected pending STAT CT
  • Any bleed in a critical anatomical site — intracranial, intraspinal, intraocular, retroperitoneal, pericardial, or intramuscular with compartment syndrome
  • Ongoing bleeding causing haemodynamic instability or respiratory compromise
  • Massive GI bleeding
  • Airway compromise from oropharyngeal or neck haematoma
  • Platelet <10–20 ×109/L WITH active critical bleeding
  • Need for continuous/repeated platelet transfusion to hold any increment
  • Anti-D-induced intravascular haemolysis with multi-organ dysfunction, ARDS or DIC
  • Consideration of emergency splenectomy
Do not wait for the platelet count to justify the transfer. The 2026 emergency guideline's population is a platelet count <20 ×109/L plus bleeding that threatens life or major organ function — but the bleeding is the trigger, not the number. A patient at 35 with an expanding intracranial bleed belongs in the unit; a patient at 6 who is dry does not.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness — all of these

CriterionThreshold / detail
Bleeding has stoppedNo new bleeding; stable haemoglobin.
Platelet count rising and in a safe range>20–30 ×109/L AND trending UP — the trend matters as much as the value. Pragmatic synthesis: matches ICR 2019's treatment goal (>20–30 for symptomatic patients) and ASH 2019's outpatient threshold (≥20). No guideline specifies a formal safe-to-discharge platelet threshold — this is synthesis, not a graded recommendation.
Diagnosis is secureSecondary causes screened; film reviewed; TTP excluded.
Follow-up arrangedHaematology, with a CBC within ~1 week. Not "call the office" — an actual appointment.
Steroid taper written with an explicit STOP DATE≤6 weeks total including taper (ASH 2019 STRONG). Put the stop date in the discharge summary. This is precisely where prolonged-steroid harm originates — a taper with no end written by an inpatient team the outpatient doctor never speaks to.
Patient educatedBleeding precautions; when to return (headache, wet purpura, any major bleed); drugs to avoid (aspirin/NSAIDs); quinine is in tonic water.
A plan for when the IVIG wears offIf the count is being held up by IVIG alone, name the agent that will hold it at week 3 before they leave.

Disposition

Most ITP patients go home. ITP is not a functional-decline disease — it does not, by itself, produce the deconditioning that drives SNF/IRF/LTAC placement. When a higher level of care is needed, it is almost always because of what the bleeding did (an ICH), not the ITP.

Home

The default. Bleeding stopped, count >20–30 and rising, diagnosis secure, haematology follow-up with a CBC in ~1 week, taper stop-date written.

Home health / infusion centre

For IVIG courses or scheduled infusions; nursing for those who cannot reliably return for counts. Also useful for the elderly patient on a steroid taper needing glucose/BP checks.

SNF

Rarely for ITP itself. Consider for the frail elderly deconditioned by a prolonged admission, or needing 24h skilled nursing after a bleed. ⚠️ Fall risk + thrombocytopenia is a dangerous pairing — ensure the facility knows the count and the precautions.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Post-ICH. Can tolerate ≥3h therapy/day across ≥2 disciplines. The ITP is incidental — the neuro deficit is the reason. 16.2% of critical-bleed survivors have neurologic sequelae.

LTAC

Prolonged complex care >25 days — e.g. vent weaning after a catastrophic ICH. Not an ITP disposition; an ICH-complication disposition.

Hospice / palliative

Devastating ICH with poor prognosis; or refractory ITP with uncontrollable bleeding in a patient who has exhausted mechanistically distinct options. Goals-of-care conversations belong here too — ~30% adult mortality in critical bleeding is a number families deserve to hear.
The second-line decision happens in clinic, not on the wards — but you set it up. The inpatient team's most durable contribution is a secure diagnosis, a steroid course with an end date, and a haematology appointment that actually exists. Whether this patient ends up on a TPO-RA, rituximab or a splenectomy is decided over months by someone else — but if you discharge them with an open-ended prednisone script and no appointment, you have chosen for them: they will be steroid-dependent, and steroid-dependence is non-response.
🫀 ICU — critical & life-threatening bleeding
Admit

ICU triggers & the critical bleed

🚨

What counts as a "critical bleed" — and why ASH 2019 can't help you here

ASH 2019 explicitly does NOT cover this. Verbatim from the guideline: it does "not address emergency management of ITP, pregnancy, or treatments that were introduced after 2017." If you are managing a critical ITP bleed, ASH 2019 is the wrong document. Use the 2026 ASH/McMaster emergency guideline (Chowdhury, Arnold et al, Blood Adv 2026, PMID 41637560) and ICR 2019. This is not a technicality — it is why so much bedside teaching on emergency ITP is folklore.

Definition — verbatim from the systematic review underpinning the guideline

Critical bleed"A bleed in a critical anatomical site including intracranial, intraspinal, intraocular, retroperitoneal, pericardial, or intramuscular with compartment syndrome; OR an ongoing bleed that results in haemodynamic instability or respiratory compromise."

The 2026 guideline's population: adults and children with ITP, a platelet count <20 ×109/L, and bleeding serious enough to threaten life or major organ function.

Why this is a true emergency — the outcome data

From the systematic review (49 studies, 112 critical-bleed ITP patients: 66 children [median age 10], 36 adults [median 41.5], 10 unreported):

OutcomeRate
Overall mortality25%
ADULT mortality30.6%
Paediatric mortality19.7%
Bleeding resolution81.7%
Neurologic disability / sequelae in survivors16.2%
Mortality with COMBINATION therapy21.7%
Mortality with a SINGLE intervention30.2%
Roughly 1 in 3 adults with a critical ITP bleed dies. This is not a "trend the count and see" situation. And note the last two rows: combination therapy 21.7% vs single intervention 30.2%. That single comparison is the entire mechanistic and clinical argument for throwing everything at it simultaneously rather than sequentially. Sequential therapy is how you lose this patient politely.

ICU triggers

  • Confirmed or suspected ICH (suspected = STAT CT and start treating)
  • Any critical-site bleed per the definition above
  • Haemodynamic instability or respiratory compromise from bleeding
  • Airway compromise — oropharyngeal/neck haematoma
  • Need for continuous platelet transfusion
  • Anti-D-induced intravascular haemolysis with MODS/ARDS/DIC
  • Consideration of emergency splenectomy
Rescue

The 2026 rescue bundle

⚽

GIVE EVERYTHING. GIVE IT TOGETHER. NOW.

The 2026 guideline's central recommendation. Despite low-certainty evidence, the panel issued STRONG recommendations for combined treatment with high-dose corticosteroids, high-dose IVIG, platelet transfusions, tranexamic acid, and a TPO-receptor agonist — "used together or very close together." The panel explicitly cited the "life-threatening nature of the condition" as the reason for issuing strong recommendations on weak evidence.
Notice the unusual GRADE construction: STRONG recommendations despite LOW-certainty evidence. This is a recognised GRADE paradigm — when the harm is catastrophic and irreversible and the intervention is available, you act. Do not let the phrase "low certainty" talk you out of treating aggressively. The evidence is weak because nobody can randomise a patient with an intracranial bleed and a platelet count of 4; it is not weak because the treatment doesn't work.

The bundle — all five, together

#ComponentDoseWhy it's in the bundle
1High-dose corticosteroidIV methylprednisolone 1 g daily ×3 days
OR IV dexamethasone 40 mg daily ×4 days		Maximal, immediate suppression of macrophage FcγR phagocytosis + antibody production. Slow to peak, so it cannot be the only thing you do.
2High-dose IVIG1 g/kg ×1–2 consecutive days (total up to 2 g/kg)The fastest immunologic lever you have — onset 1–3 days. Saturates the FcγR so the platelets you transfuse (and the ones they still make) survive. Review mortality 14.3%, platelet response 88% — the best of any single agent reported.
3Platelet transfusionGive it — and repeat it. Often continuous because of ongoing immune consumption."Even though the increment may not last." In ICH, transfuse until the IVIG takes effect. ICR 2019: platelet transfusions are "not to be postponed." This is the one setting where the ITP transfusion taboo is suspended.
4Tranexamic acid15–20 mg/kg every 8 hours (ICR 2019)Antifibrinolytic — stabilises whatever clot they manage to form. ⚠️ Caution/avoid in haematuria (clot retention → obstruction). No RCT has evaluated TXA specifically in ITP.
5TPO-receptor agonistStandard starting doses (romiplostim 1 mcg/kg SC weekly · eltrombopag 50 mg PO daily · avatrombopag 20 mg PO daily) — see Drug referenceStart it on day 1, not day 5. It takes 5–14 days to work — which is exactly when the IVIG will be wearing off and the steroids tapering. It is the bridge to durable recovery. In the review, TPO-RA had a 100% platelet response in the 17 reported critical-bleed patients (tiny N — do not over-read).
6Urgent splenectomyCONDITIONAL recommendation — if initial treatments failRemoves the clearance site immediately — the only intervention with an instant mechanical effect. Review mortality in the splenectomy subgroup 28.6%, heavily confounded by indication (these were the sickest patients who had already failed everything).
Why the bundle is a bundle — read it as a relay, not a pile. Each component covers a different time window:
• Platelet transfusion works in minutes — and is destroyed in hours.
• IVIG works in 1–3 days — and blockades the FcγR so the next transfusion actually survives. (This is why transfusion + IVIG together beats either alone: IVIG makes the transfusion work.)
• Steroids work in 4–14 days — holding the ground IVIG took.
• TPO-RA works in 5–14 days — rebuilding actual production for when everything else wears off.
• TXA works continuously, on the clot itself, independent of platelet number.
Give them sequentially and each one arrives after the patient needed it. That is what the 21.7% vs 30.2% mortality difference is measuring.
⛔ DO NOT USE — two agents that survive in teaching but not in the guidelines
AgentWhy not
Recombinant factor VIIa (rFVIIa)The 2026 guideline advised AGAINST rFVIIa because of thrombosis risk, and ICR 2019 also lists it among NOT-recommended emergency measures. It appears in older "in extremis" algorithms and in IWG 2009's list of adjunctive (non-ITP-specific) therapies — which is how it entered the folklore. Neither current consensus document endorses it, and the newest one explicitly rejects it.
Plasmapheresis / plasma exchangeICR 2019 lists it as NOT recommended in ITP. It is the treatment for TTP. Reaching for PLEX in ITP usually means someone has confused the two diseases — which is a reason to re-examine the diagnosis, not to start the machine.

Other options ICR 2019 mentions for emergencies: high-dose methylprednisolone; vinca alkaloids (vincristine 1–2 mg or vinblastine 10 mg weekly — "rapid, peak effect in 7–9 days"); IV anti-D; antifibrinolytics combined with other initial therapies; and, rarely, emergency splenectomy. Combining prednisone with IVIG and/or IV anti-D may elicit a response in patients refractory to single agents alone.

Reverse

Reversing anticoagulants & antiplatelets

🛡️

There is no ITP-specific reversal guideline — use standard agent-specific reversal, aggressively

The compounded defect is the point: a thrombocytopenic patient on an anticoagulant has lost both primary and secondary haemostasis. Reverse fast and completely.

AgentReversal
Warfarin4-factor PCC + IV vitamin K 10 mg (PCC works in minutes; vitamin K prevents the rebound in hours — you need both)
DabigatranIdarucizumab 5 g IV
Rivaroxaban / apixabanAndexanet alfa, or 4-factor PCC if unavailable
UFHProtamine sulfate
LMWHProtamine (partial reversal only — do not assume full effect)
Aspirin / P2Y12 inhibitorsSTOP. Platelet transfusion is of debated benefit in ICH on antiplatelets generally (PATCH trial found transfusion was associated with worse outcomes in spontaneous ICH on antiplatelets) — but in ITP with a critical bleed, platelet transfusion is recommended regardless by the 2026 guideline. Different problem: PATCH patients had normal counts and inhibited platelets; your patient has almost no platelets at all.
ThrombolyticsCryoprecipitate ± TXA

Also: stop all NSAIDs; hold VTE pharmacoprophylaxis (use SCDs); and correct any coexisting coagulopathy — which should immediately prompt you to ask whether this is really ITP at all, or DIC.

Monitor

Monitoring, access & airway

🩸

Lines, labs, targets — and the procedures that will hurt them

DomainAction
PlateletsQ6–12 h initially, and after each transfusion — the increment (or its absence) tells you how fast they are consuming.
CBC / HgbQ6–12 h — ongoing loss, transfusion needs.
Neuro checksHourly if ICH or at risk. Low threshold for repeat non-contrast head CT — haematoma expansion is the thing you are watching for.
Coags (PT/aPTT/fibrinogen)Confirm this is not DIC; monitor during massive transfusion.
FibrinogenKeep >150 mg/dL if massively transfusing.
Type & crossmatchKeep active. ⚠️ If anti-D was given and transfusion is needed → use Rh(D)-NEGATIVE red cells (per the WinRho boxed warning) so you do not feed the haemolysis.
Renal functionIVIG nephrotoxicity (boxed warning); haemolysis.
GlucoseHigh-dose steroids. ⚠️ Anti-D's 10% maltose causes falsely high glucometer readings — confirm on a lab glucose before treating.
VASCULAR ACCESS — where you put the needle matters more than usual.
• Prefer peripheral IVs. If a central line is unavoidable, use a COMPRESSIBLE site — femoral or internal jugular over subclavian, because the subclavian cannot be compressed if you lacerate it. That single anatomical fact should drive the choice.
• Ultrasound guidance is mandatory.
• Correct the count FIRST if the line is not emergent.
• Avoid arterial lines, lumbar punctures and IM injections until the count is safe.
• Avoid nasal intubation — epistaxis in a patient who cannot clot it.

Airway & respiratory support — when it's relevant

ITP does not cause respiratory failure. The bleeding does — via a depressed GCS from ICH, an expanding neck/oropharyngeal haematoma, or ARDS from anti-D-induced intravascular haemolysis. Intubate for those, not for the platelet count.

Intubate when
GCS ≤8
or airway compromise from haematoma — early, before it's an emergency
Route
ORAL only
⛔ nasal intubation contraindicated — epistaxis
Mode
AC/VC
lung-protective 6 mL/kg IBW
If ICH
PaCO₂ 35–40
avoid hypercapnia (↑ICP); avoid prophylactic hyperventilation
Oxygenation
SpO₂ 92–96%
avoid hypoxia — secondary brain injury
If anti-D given
Watch for ARDS
named in the boxed warning as an IVH complication
On pressorsITP is not a shock state. If your ITP patient needs vasopressors, they are in haemorrhagic shock (or something else is going on — sepsis, anti-D haemolysis with MODS). The treatment for haemorrhagic shock is blood and source control, not noradrenaline; pressors are a bridge while you resuscitate, not a therapy. Use standard haemorrhagic-shock management — there is nothing ITP-specific about it, and no ITP guideline addresses pressors.
Refractory

When the bundle fails

⚙️

Still bleeding, count still unmeasurable — what's left

  1. Re-examine the diagnosis. Now. A patient who does not respond to the full bundle may not have ITP. Is this TTP? (schistocytes, LDH, ADAMTS13 — and you have been withholding the plasma exchange that would save them). Is this DIC? (coags). Is this HIT? (heparin, thrombosis). Is this marrow failure/leukaemia? Non-response is a diagnostic finding.
  2. Urgent splenectomy — the 2026 guideline's conditional recommendation when initial treatments fail. It is the only intervention that removes the clearance organ instantly.
  3. Vinca alkaloids — vincristine 1–2 mg or vinblastine 10 mg weekly. Peak effect 7–9 days (ICR 2019). A real option in the refractory emergency.
  4. Add IV anti-D to steroids — if Rh(D)+, non-splenectomised, DAT−, not haemolysing. (Note the contradiction to manage: if you are contemplating urgent splenectomy, anti-D stops working the moment the spleen is out.)
  5. Continuous platelet transfusion — not a bolus. Ongoing consumption needs ongoing supply while the immunologic agents take hold.
  6. Consider the liver. If they have failed steroids, IVIG and splenectomy — every one of which targets the spleen/FcγR axis — their platelets may be dying in the liver via Ashwell–Morell desialylation-mediated clearance, which none of those drugs touch. This is the mechanistic rationale for oseltamivir (investigational, off-label; 66.6% response in multirefractory patients, but only combined with a TPO-RA or immunosuppressant).
  7. Neurosurgical consultation for ICH — but recognise the bind: you cannot operate on a platelet count of 5, and ICR 2019's target for major neurosurgery is ≥100 ×109/L. The bundle is what buys the operation.
The most important refractory manoeuvre is not a drug — it is re-reading the film. The McMaster registry found 12.2% of "primary ITP" was something else, and misdiagnosed patients were the ones who didn't behave as expected. In the unit, at 3am, with a patient bleeding into their head and not responding to everything you own, "what if this isn't ITP" is the highest-yield thought available to you.
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor — ALL of these, not most

Transfer out of ICU when ALL of:
  • Bleeding has stopped — no new bleeding for ≥24 h, stable haemoglobin, no transfusion requirement
  • Platelet count rising and sustained >30–50 ×109/L without continuous platelet transfusion
  • Neurologically stable with stable or improving imaging if ICH
  • Haemodynamically stable, off vasopressors
  • No further need for continuous platelet transfusion
  • A definitive second-line plan is RUNNING — TPO-RA started, rituximab given, or splenectomy done/planned
Sourcing honestyNo guideline specifies a formal ICU downgrade threshold for ITP — the >30–50 figure is synthesis, not a graded recommendation. It is anchored on ICR 2019's treatment goal (>20–30 ×109/L for symptomatic patients) and the 2026 guideline's entry criterion (<20 ×109/L), set deliberately above both because a patient who just bled into their brain deserves more margin than a patient who never did.
"Not yet" — do NOT downgrade if:
• The count is being held up ONLY by treatments that are about to stop. IVIG lasts 2–4 weeks and the steroids are being tapered. A count of 60 on day 3 post-IVIG with nothing else running is a countdown, not a recovery. This is the single most important downgrade error in ITP.
• They still need any platelet transfusion to hold an increment.
• The ICH has not been re-imaged or is still expanding.
• The diagnosis is still uncertain — if you are not sure this is ITP, the floor is not the place to find out.
• There is no haematology plan for the next 2 weeks.
The whole downgrade logic in one sentence: the acute agents are a blockade and the TPO-RA is a rebuild — you may only leave the unit once the rebuild has started, because the blockade has an expiry date.
Shared

Drug reference — every agent, full ladder

📋

Boxed warnings at a glance — frequently misremembered

All doses below are from current FDA-approved labelling (DailyMed = the FDA-submitted SPL) unless explicitly attributed to a guideline. Where guideline and label disagree, both are shown and the discrepancy is flagged.

DrugBoxed warning?Contraindications
Eltrombopag (Promacta)✅ YES — hepatotoxicity component APPLIES to ITP—
Rituximab (Rituxan)✅ YES — 4 componentsNone
Anti-D (WinRho SDF)✅ YES — intravascular haemolysisSeveral
IVIG (class)✅ YES — thrombosis, renal dysfunction/ARFProduct-specific
Romiplostim (Nplate)❌ NONone
Avatrombopag (Doptelet)❌ NONone
Fostamatinib (Tavalisse)❌ NONone
Rilzabrutinib (Wayrilz)❌ NONone
Only 4 of 8 carry a boxed warning — and the three newer oral agents (avatrombopag, fostamatinib, rilzabrutinib) plus romiplostim have none, all with "Contraindications: None." The reflex that "the new drugs must be the dangerous ones" is exactly backwards here: the boxed warnings sit on the old, familiar agents — IVIG, anti-D, rituximab and eltrombopag.
📡

TPO-receptor agonists — the agents with real ladders

All three stimulate c-Mpl to increase platelet PRODUCTION — they supply the signal the body failed to send. They do nothing about the destruction, which is exactly why the count falls again when you stop. All three: target the lowest dose achieving ≥50 ×109/L; carry thrombotic warnings; and require weekly CBC after discontinuation (rebound thrombocytopenia).

"Do not use PROMACTA to normalize platelet counts." — verbatim from the label, and true of the whole class. The target is 50, not 250. You are buying haemostatic safety, not a normal number. Overshooting is where the thrombosis risk lives.

Eltrombopag (Promacta / Revolade) — oral daily

BOXED WARNING — and yes, it reaches ITP. Title verbatim: "WARNING: RISK FOR HEPATIC DECOMPENSATION IN PATIENTS WITH CHRONIC HEPATITIS C and RISK OF HEPATOTOXICITY." The hepatic-decompensation component is HCV-specific; the hepatotoxicity component applies to ALL indications including ITP: "PROMACTA may increase the risk of severe and potentially life-threatening hepatotoxicity."
PopulationSTARTING dose
Adults + children ≥6 yr50 mg PO once daily
Children 1–5 yr25 mg once daily
East-/Southeast-Asian ancestry (≥6 yr)25 mg once daily
Hepatic impairment — Child-Pugh A, B or C25 mg once daily — ⚠️ note this includes MILD (Child-Pugh A)
BOTH Asian ancestry + hepatic impairmentConsider 12.5 mg once daily
Two corrections to common teaching: ① The label says "East-/Southeast-Asian ancestry" — broader than "East Asian." ② The hepatic dose reduction applies to ANY hepatic impairment including Child-Pugh A (mild), not just moderate/severe.
TITRATION LADDER (Label Table 1)Action
<50 after ≥2 weeks↑ daily dose by 25 mg to max 75 mg/day. (If on 12.5 mg → go to 25 mg first, THEN increment by 25 mg)
≥200 to ≤400↓ daily dose by 25 mg; wait 2 weeks. (If on 25 mg → 12.5 mg)
>400STOP; monitor twice weekly. When <150, restart at a dose reduced by 25 mg
>400 after 2 weeks at the lowest doseDISCONTINUE

Ladder in one line: 25 → 50 → 75 mg/day (max). Target: lowest dose maintaining ≥50. Stop for non-response after 4 weeks at 75 mg/day.

⚠️ ADMINISTRATION — TWO SEPARATE RULES; DO NOT MERGE THEM.
1. Food: take "without a meal or with a meal low in calcium (≤50 mg)."
2. Cations (chelation): take "at least 2 HOURS BEFORE or 4 HOURS AFTER any medications or products containing polyvalent cations, such as antacids, calcium-rich foods, and mineral supplements."

This is the #1 practical reason eltrombopag "fails." Polyvalent cations (Ca²⁺, Fe²⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺, Zn²⁺) chelate eltrombopag and destroy its absorption. A patient taking it with breakfast, milk, a calcium supplement, iron or an antacid is effectively not being treated. Always ask how they take it before you escalate the dose. Memorise the asymmetry: 2 hours before / 4 hours after.

MONITORING: ALT, AST, bilirubin at BASELINE, q2 weeks during dose adjustment, MONTHLY once stable. After discontinuation: CBC weekly ×≥4 weeks.
W&P: hepatotoxicity; ↑risk of death and progression of MDS→AML; thrombotic events; cataracts; lab test interference.
Long-term safety (EXTEND, n=302, median exposure 2.37 yr, up to 8.76 yr): 85.8% achieved a platelet response ≥50 at least once; 52% had a continuous response ≥25 weeks; bleeding fell from 57% to 16% at 1 year; thromboembolic events 6%, hepatobiliary AEs 15% — and critically, neither rate increased with treatment beyond 1 year.

Romiplostim (Nplate) — subcutaneous weekly

No boxed warning. Contraindications: None.

START: 1 mcg/kg SC once weekly (adults and children ≥1 yr — same). Increment: 1 mcg/kg. MAX: 10 mcg/kg/week. Use actual body weight at initiation.

Platelet count (×109/L)Action
<50↑ by 1 mcg/kg
>200 and ≤400 for 2 CONSECUTIVE weeks↓ by 1 mcg/kg
>400DO NOT DOSE. Assess weekly. When <200, resume at a dose reduced by 1 mcg/kg

Ladder: 1 → 2 → 3 … → 10 mcg/kg/week (max). Stop for non-response after 4 weeks at 10 mcg/kg. MONITORING: CBC weekly during titration, monthly once stable; weekly ×≥2 weeks after discontinuation.

⚠️ Two trap differences vs eltrombopag/avatrombopag — these are exam favourites and real-world errors:
① The resume threshold after >400 is <200 for Nplate — vs <150 for Promacta and Doptelet.
② The >200 dose reduction requires 2 CONSECUTIVE weeks for Nplate; Promacta reduces at any single reading in the 200–400 window.
The ~14-day lag. There is roughly a two-week delay between a romiplostim dose change and its maximal effect. This is the cause of the classic overshoot/undershoot oscillation — you chase a low count up, overshoot to 500, hold, crash, chase again. Change the dose and then WAIT. The patient who oscillates is usually being titrated by someone impatient.
⚠️ Honest gap: the label specifies weight reassessment q12 weeks for paediatrics only. I could not verify an explicit adult weight-reassessment interval and am not inventing one.

Avatrombopag (Doptelet) — oral daily, with food

No boxed warning. Contraindications: None. NO LFT monitoring requirement and NO hepatotoxicity warning — the main practical differentiator vs eltrombopag. Only W&P listed: thrombotic/thromboembolic complications.

FOOD: "Administer DOPTELET tablets WITH FOOD." — ⚠️ the exact opposite of eltrombopag, and there is no cation-separation rule. Two drugs in the same class with opposite administration instructions is a genuine dispensing hazard. Eltrombopag: empty stomach, dodge the calcium. Avatrombopag: with food, ignore the calcium.

CHRONIC ITP — START: 20 mg (1 tablet) once daily = DOSE LEVEL 4. Max 40 mg/day.

LevelRegimen
120 mg once weekly
220 mg twice weekly OR 40 mg once weekly
320 mg three times weekly
420 mg ONCE DAILY ← STARTING DOSE
540 mg three times weekly AND 20 mg on the four remaining days
640 mg once daily
⚠️ Correction to common teaching: the range is often described as "20 mg 3×/week up to 40 mg daily." The actual label ladder spans 20 mg ONCE WEEKLY (Level 1) to 40 mg once daily (Level 6), with the start at Level 4 — meaning most of the titration room is DOWNWARD. There is far more room to de-escalate than most people realise, which matters because the whole class is about finding the lowest effective dose.
Platelet count (×109/L)Action (Label Table 2)
<50 after ≥2 weeks↑ one dose level; wait 2 weeks
200–400↓ one dose level; wait 2 weeks
>400STOP; monitor twice weekly; when <150, ↓ one level and reinitiate
<50 after 4 weeks at 40 mg daily (Level 6)DISCONTINUE
>400 after 2 weeks at 20 mg weekly (Level 1)DISCONTINUE

MONITORING: platelets weekly until stable ≥50, then monthly; weekly ×≥4 weeks after stopping.
⚠️ INTERACTIONS change the STARTING dose: moderate/strong dual CYP2C9 + CYP3A4 INHIBITORS → start at Level 3 (20 mg three times weekly); moderate/strong dual INDUCERS → start at Level 6 (40 mg once daily).
Paediatrics: ≥6 yr → 20 mg daily; 1–<6 yr (SPRINKLE granules) → 10 mg daily, max 20 mg/day.

⚠️ DO NOT CROSS-APPLY THE CHRONIC-LIVER-DISEASE INDICATION. Avatrombopag's other indication — thrombocytopenia in CLD before a procedure — is a completely different, fixed regimen: dose by baseline platelet (<40 → 60 mg daily ×5 days; 40 to <50 → 40 mg daily ×5 days), "begin dosing 10 to 13 days prior to the scheduled procedure", with the procedure "5 to 8 days after the last dose." No titration, no platelet target. Commonly misremembered as "5 days pre-procedure" — it is 5 days of DOSING, begun 10–13 days before.

How to actually choose:
• Hates needles / wants a pill → eltrombopag or avatrombopag.
• Chaotic diet, takes calcium/iron, or you suspect non-adherence to the fasting rule → avatrombopag (with food, no cation dance).
• Any liver disease, or HCV → avoid eltrombopag or reduce to 25 mg; avatrombopag has no hepatotox warning.
• Won't come for monthly LFTs → avatrombopag.
• Wants the biggest evidence base / weekly clinic contact is a feature not a bug → romiplostim.
• The avatrombopag pitch in one line: same class, no fasting, no cation dance, no LFT monitoring, no boxed warning — at the cost of the smallest evidence base (phase 3 N=49).

Thrombosis risk — the honest answer

Balancing a real warning against real data • All three labels carry thrombotic warnings, and avatrombopag's phase 3 had 3/32 (9.4%) thromboembolic events in a tiny N.
• But a systematic review/meta-analysis of RCTs found NO statistically significant increase for any agent: romiplostim OR 0.92 (0.14–6.13); eltrombopag OR 2.32 (0.64–8.47); avatrombopag OR 4.15 (0.20–85.23). Look at those confidence intervals — the trials are simply underpowered for this question.
• EXTEND showed the eltrombopag TEE rate (6%) did not increase beyond 1 year.
• Confounder: ITP itself carries increased thrombotic risk, independent of treatment.

The balanced read: the signal is biologically plausible and label-warned, but RCT meta-analysis does not confirm a significant excess. Do NOT refuse a TPO-RA to a bleeding patient out of thrombosis fear. DO avoid overshooting the count, and DO weigh it carefully in prior thrombosis, APS, or strong risk factors.

Stopping — and the myth that TPO-RAs are never curative

"TPO-RAs are not curative" is only half true — and the best data say roughly HALF can stop. Sustained remission off treatment (SROT) after a planned, structured taper is reported across a wide range: a consensus range of ~25–40%; 30.5% in TAPER (n=105, eltrombopag given early after steroid failure); and 52.1% at 1 year — still 47.9% after 4+ more years of follow-up — in STOPAGO (n=48, patients tapered off after an established stable response), with 39.6% in sustained COMPLETE remission at that point. Only chronic (vs persistent) ITP at initiation predicted a non-sustained response.
The honest caveat: every one of these studies is single-arm or observational — no randomised trial of TPO-RA discontinuation exists. The spread (30% vs 52%) largely reflects who was tapered: patients with a long-established complete response do far better than those tapered early.
Practical: taper, don't stop abruptly — and check a CBC weekly for 2–4 weeks after stopping, because rebound thrombocytopenia can dip BELOW the original baseline. The question "should we try stopping?" deserves to be asked of every stable patient, not assumed away.
💊

Fostamatinib & rilzabrutinib — the targeted orals

Fostamatinib (Tavalisse) — Syk inhibitor

Spleen tyrosine kinase (Syk) inhibitor — blocks the signal immediately downstream of the FcγR in macrophages, so the receptor can still bind the antibody but the cell never gets the order to eat. Cut the wire between the inspector's scanner and his hands.

No boxed warning. Contraindications: None. Take with or without food.

START: 100 mg PO BID.
ESCALATE (verbatim): "After a month, if platelet count has not increased to at least 50 ×109/L, increase TAVALISSE dose to 150 mg twice daily." MAX 150 mg BID (300 mg/day).
STOP FOR NON-RESPONSE: discontinue after 12 weeks if platelets haven't reached a level sufficient to avoid clinically important bleeding.

⚠️ Correction: the escalation trigger is "at least 50" (≥50), not ">50."

DOSE-REDUCTION LADDER (for toxicity): 300 mg/day (150 BID) → 200 mg/day (100 BID) → 150 mg/day (150 mg AM only) → 100 mg/day (100 mg AM only) → below 100 mg/day: DISCONTINUE.

ToxicityRule
HepatotoxicityALT/AST 3–5× ULN → interrupt, resume lower if symptomatic. ≥5× ULN with bili <2× ULN → interrupt; resume lower, or discontinue if persists ≥2 wk. ALT/AST ≥3× ULN + bilirubin >2× ULN → DISCONTINUE
HypertensionStage 1 (130–139/80–89) → start/↑ antihypertensive; reduce fostamatinib if uncontrolled after 8 wk. Stage 2 (≥140/≥90) → if persists ≥8 wk, reduce dose; if ≥160/100 for ≥4 wk despite therapy → interrupt/discontinue. Crisis (>180/>120) → interrupt/discontinue
DiarrhoeaGrade ≥3 → interrupt; resume at next lower dose when back to Grade 1
NeutropeniaANC <1.0 ×109/L persisting >72 h → interrupt until ANC >1.5; resume next lower dose

MONITORING: BP q2 weeks until a stable dose is reached, then monthly; LFTs monthly; CBC monthly until stable ≥50.
INTERACTIONS: strong CYP3A4 inhibitor → ↑R406 exposure, may need dose modification. Strong CYP3A4 inducer → NOT RECOMMENDED. Fostamatinib ↑ CYP3A4, BCRP and P-gp substrates → watch statins (esp. simvastatin) and digoxin.
Embryo-fetal toxicity: contraception during + 1 month after.
Efficacy (FIT1/FIT2 pooled, n=150, median ITP duration 8.5 years): stable response 18% (18/101) vs 2% (1/49) placebo, P=0.0003; overall response 43% vs 14%, P=0.0006; median time to response 15 days. Safety: diarrhoea 31% vs 15%; hypertension 28% vs 13%; ALT elevation 11% vs 0%.

Set expectations honestly: an 18% stable response is modest. But it was achieved in patients with a median 8.5 years of ITP who had failed everything — and it works by a mechanism no other approved oral agent uses. That is the argument for it: not potency, orthogonality. (Minor sourcing note: the FDA label reports the FIT2 stable-response count as 8/50 (16%) where the journal reports 9/50 (18%) — a one-patient discrepancy.)

Rilzabrutinib (Wayrilz) — BTK inhibitor — NEWLY APPROVED

✅ FDA-approved 29 August 2025 — the FIRST BTK inhibitor approved for ITPIndication (verbatim): "adult patients with persistent or chronic immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) who have had an insufficient response to a previous treatment." This post-dates every current guideline — ASH 2019, ICR 2019 and the 2026 emergency guideline all pre-date or exclude it.
A reversible, covalent BTK inhibitor with a genuinely dual mechanism: BTK sits in both the FcγR signalling pathway in macrophages (blocking phagocytosis) and the B-cell receptor pathway (reducing autoantibody production) — without depleting B cells and without impairing platelet aggregation. Cut the wire AND turn down the printers, without burning down the print shop. That last point is why bleeding decreased rather than increased, which is counterintuitive for a BTK inhibitor.

DOSE: 400 mg PO twice daily. FIXED — no titration, no platelet-guided adjustment, no dose-modification table. With or without food; swallow whole — do not cut, crush or chew.
No boxed warning. Contraindications: None. No time-based discontinuation rule for non-response is stated in the label.
WARNINGS: serious infections (fatal pneumonia occurred); hepatotoxicity including DILI; embryo-fetal toxicity (contraception during + 1 week after).
MONITORING: bilirubin + transaminases at baseline and as clinically indicated.

⚠️ INTERACTIONS — the PPI trap.
• AVOID PPIs ENTIRELY — pH-dependent solubility means a PPI simply switches the drug off. This is a very real trap: a large share of ITP patients are on steroids + a PPI for gastroprotection. Check the med list before you prescribe.
• Antacids/H2RAs: give Wayrilz ≥2 hours BEFORE.
• Avoid strong OR moderate CYP3A inhibitors AND inducers. Rilzabrutinib is itself a moderate CYP3A inhibitor.
• ORGAN IMPAIRMENT: AVOID in moderate–severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh B–C) and in severe renal impairment.

LUNA 3 (phase 3) — Kuter et al, Blood 2025;145(24):2914–2926 (note: Blood, not NEJM). Phase 3, double-blind, 2:1, N=202 (133 rilzabrutinib / 69 placebo), 24-week blinded period. Median ITP duration 7.7 years; median 4 prior therapies; 28% prior splenectomy.

  • Primary endpoint — durable platelet response: 23% (31/133) vs 0% (0/69), P<0.0001
  • Platelet response (≥50 at 2 consecutive visits): 40% vs 9%
  • Median time to first platelet ≥50: 15 days
  • Rescue therapy 33% vs 58% — a 52% reduction, P=0.0007
  • Fatigue improved (P=0.0003); bleeding improved (P=0.0006)
  • Safety: all grade 1–2 diarrhoea 23% vs 4%, nausea 17% vs 6%. Grade ≥2 bleeding 4% vs 12% — i.e. LESS bleeding despite BTK inhibition.
⚠️ Use 23%, not 29%. Some secondary sources report 29% — that figure comes from a later, interim analysis combining the double-blind AND open-label extension periods (where placebo patients cross over, so there is no comparator). The peer-reviewed registrational primary endpoint is 23% vs 0%. Do not substitute one for the other.
🦠

Rituximab & splenectomy

Rituximab — OFF-LABEL for ITP

ITP is NOT an FDA-approved indication for rituximab. Approved indications are NHL, CLL, RA, GPA, MPA and pemphigus vulgaris. All ITP use is off-label, and neither ITP regimen appears in the label.
Anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody → depletes B cells → fewer short-lived plasma cells → less autoantibody. Step 1 of the cascade — the sticker-printing shop. Note what it does not do: existing antibody must still decay, which is why it is slow.
RegimenDetail
375 mg/m² IV weekly ×4 dosesThe best-studied regimen per ASH 2019
1000 mg IV on day 1 and day 15Fixed-dose alternative
100 mg weekly ×4 (low-dose)Described in ICR 2019

ASH 2019 notes there is NO prospective head-to-head comparison of these regimens. For orientation: the label uses 375 mg/m² weekly ×4 for NHL/GPA/MPA, and two 1000 mg infusions 2 weeks apart for RA and pemphigus — the ITP regimens are extrapolated from these.

BOXED WARNING — all four components:
• Fatal infusion-related reactions within 24 h — ~80% of fatal reactions occurred with the FIRST infusion.
• Severe mucocutaneous reactions, some fatal.
• HBV reactivation — fulminant hepatitis, hepatic failure and death.
• Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) resulting in death.
🔴 HBV SCREENING IS MANDATORY (verbatim): "Screen ALL patients for HBV infection by measuring HBsAg AND anti-HBc before initiating treatment." Monitor carriers during and for several months following therapy — reactivation has been reported up to 24 MONTHS after completion.

It is HBsAg AND anti-HBc. Anti-HBc catches the resolved/occult carrier who is HBsAg-negative but still at risk of reactivation. Checking only HBsAg is the classic, potentially fatal miss. ICR 2019: those with active infection needing rituximab should receive concurrent antiviral treatment.

Other: Contraindications: None. Premedicate with acetaminophen + an antihistamine (many add a corticosteroid). Live virus vaccines are not recommended before or during treatment — and vaccinate against encapsulated organisms BEFORE (ICR 2019, Grade C).
Efficacy: ~60% overall response; 20–25% durable (ICR 2019). Per the pathogenesis literature: 40% at 1 year, 30% at 5 years, ~40% non-responders. Time to response is SLOW: initial 7–56 d, peak 14–180 d. This is not a rescue drug.

Why it relapses — a beautiful piece of mechanism. After rituximab, memory T-follicular-helper cells persist in the spleen with a modified phenotype. When B cells reconstitute, those TFH cells "recover their usual phenotype and functions" and restart the autoimmune machinery. Rituximab pauses the disease; it does not delete it. The instruction manual survives in the spleen even after you shut the factory.

Splenectomy

TIMING: defer ≥12 months from diagnosis. ASH 2019 Rec 9 remark: "If possible, splenectomy should be delayed for at least 1 year after diagnosis because of the potential for spontaneous remission in the first year." ICR 2019: ≥12–24 months.
VaccineTiming
Pneumococcal (PCV)≥14 DAYS BEFORE elective splenectomy.
Per CDC/ACIP: doses given during the 14 days before surgery can still be counted as valid; if not given before, administer as soon as the patient is stable afterwards.
Meningococcal ACWY
Meningococcal B
H. influenzae type b (Hib)

TECHNIQUE: laparoscopic is preferred (ICR 2019). Kojouri et al: mortality 1.0% (48/4955) with laparotomy vs 0.2% (3/1301) with laparoscopy; complications 12.9% vs 9.6%.

Response rates — sourceFinding
Kojouri, Blood 2004 (systematic review, 135 case series)Complete response in 1731/2623 (66%) of adults; CR rates did not correlate with duration of follow-up
IWG 2009"curative potential of splenectomy in more than 60% of cases"
ICR 2019Response up to 90% initially; 78% maintained at 10 years
Splenectomy remains the single most effective durable therapy in ITP (~60–70% durable CR) and the only one that can fairly be called curative. Its decline is not driven by lack of efficacy — it is driven by irreversibility + lifelong OPSI/thrombosis risk + the arrival of effective, reversible drugs. That is a values trade-off, not a data one. Some patients, told the numbers plainly, still choose the operation — and they are not wrong.
RiskData
OPSIRare but mortality up to 50–70%; encapsulated organisms (S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, H. influenzae). Any post-splenectomy fever is an emergency → immediate 3rd-generation cephalosporin, do not wait for cultures.
Portal/splenic vein thrombosisA recognised, important complication. ⚠️ A screening-cohort figure of ~74% circulates but reflects systematic imaging in a selected population — it should not be quoted as the clinical incidence in ITP. I could not verify a reliable ITP-specific incidence.
Long-term VTE / arterial risk"Removal of the spleen is associated with an elevated long-lasting thrombotic risk, even in patients without underlying disease."
Surgical complications9.6% laparoscopic / 12.9% open
Accessory spleen → relapseShould be sought at surgery; a cause of failure and late relapse
Age ≥60ICR 2019: associated with significantly higher rates of relapse and postoperative complications

Post-operative course: Rebound thrombocytosis is expected and predictable — counts rise 30–100%, peaking at 7–20 days post-op, then normalise over weeks–months. Post-splenectomy venous thrombosis is usually associated with counts >600–800 ×109/L and occurs in ~5%. Perioperative LMWH is the usual thromboprophylaxis. Response is assessed 1–2 months after surgery, off concomitant treatments (IWG 2009).

⚠️ If the patient is on a TPO-RA at the time of splenectomy, STOP or reduce it. You are about to remove the clearance organ while continuing to flog the marrow — a combination that has caused extreme thrombocytosis with fatal thromboembolism. Conversely, abrupt post-splenectomy withdrawal of romiplostim has caused severe rebound thrombocytopenia. Both directions are dangerous: plan the taper around the operation date, deliberately, with haematology.

Adjuncts

AdjunctDose / detail
Tranexamic acid15–20 mg/kg every 8 hours (ICR 2019). Reported ITP use 1.5–3.0 g/day. ⚠️ No RCT has evaluated TXA specifically in ITP — ICR notes antifibrinolytics "may be useful in preventing recurrent bleeding… however, the efficacy has not been evaluated by a randomized trial in ITP patients." ⚠️ Caution/avoid in haematuria (clot retention → obstruction)

⛔ AVOIDAspirin, clopidogrel/P2Y12 inhibitors, NSAIDs · IM injections · rFVIIa · plasmapheresis
Notice how many of these say "dose not verified." That is not laziness — it is the actual state of the evidence. ITP's refractory tier runs largely on practice and small series, not labels or trials. ICR 2019 itself concedes "limited data" for several. When you use them, know that you are further from the evidence than the confident tone of most textbooks suggests — and say so to the patient.

On the horizon — and what is NOT approved yet

AgentMechanismStatus as of July 2026
Efgartigimod (Vyvgart)FcRn antagonist — blocks IgG recycling → accelerates catabolism of the pathogenic autoantibody (IgA/IgM unaffected). Shred the stickers themselves.⚠️ NOT FDA-approved for ITP. Approved for ITP in JAPAN only (March 2024). ADVANCE IV was positive (22% vs 5%, P=0.032) but the subcutaneous ADVANCE SC MISSED its primary endpoint (13.7% vs 16.2%, P=0.51). The confirmatory ADVANCE-NEXT is ongoing — topline guidance has slipped twice, now H1 2027. Treat as investigational in the US. Its US-approved indications are gMG and CIDP — not ITP.
RozanolixizumabFcRn antagonistInvestigational for ITP (~50% response in early-phase work)
Anti-BAFF (belimumab) + rituximabDepletes the long-lived plasma cells in the splenic niche that rituximab alone leaves behindInvestigational — 80% response (n=15) vs 40–50% for rituximab alone
Complement inhibitors, proteasome inhibitorsBlock CDC/C3b opsonisation; deplete plasma cellsInvestigational (ICR 2019 lists them among "promising new therapies")
Efgartigimod is the one to get right in conversation. It is FDA-approved — for myasthenia gravis and CIDP — which makes it very easy to assume it is available for ITP. It is not. Its ITP approval exists only in Japan, its subcutaneous phase 3 failed, and the US confirmatory readout is not expected until 2027 at the earliest. Saying "we could use efgartigimod" on rounds is, in the US in 2026, an off-label proposal for an unapproved indication — not a treatment option.

The pearls that change what you do

💡

Fifteen things worth knowing cold

#Pearl
1Severity is defined by BLEEDING, not by the platelet count. IWG 2009's own worked example is deliberately provocative: a patient with chronic ITP, a platelet count of 2, and a few petechiae is NOT "severe" ITP. The number frightens you; the bleeding phenotype stratifies the patient.
2The STRONG recommendation is the one telling you NOT to treat. ASH 2019: treating below 30 is conditional; withholding steroids at ≥30 without bleeding is STRONG. The guideline is more confident you should withhold than that you should give. Resist the urge to fix the number.
3Six weeks of steroid. Total. Including the taper. (ASH 2019, STRONG.) If they still need steroids at week 6, they need a second-line agent, not more steroid. And steroid-dependence counts as NON-response (IWG 2009) — not as control.
4If you need the count up tomorrow, only IVIG and anti-D deliver (1–3 days). Prednisone takes 4–14 days; dexamethasone 2–14. Steroids do not work overnight, no matter how urgently you prescribe them.
5Look at the film. Every patient. Before any treatment. It costs nothing and it is the test that prevents the catastrophes: clumps (you were about to steroid a tube artifact), schistocytes (you were about to steroid a TTP), blasts/dysplasia (you were about to steroid a leukaemia or an MDS).
612.2% of "primary ITP" is something else (McMaster registry) — and MDS is the #1 impostor. The tell: misdiagnosed patients had milder counts (median 43 vs 15). The more borderline the count, the more suspicious you should be.
7Draw quantitative immunoglobulins BEFORE the IVIG. Afterwards you cannot interpret them, and you have made CVID — a real, treatable secondary cause — invisible for months.
8You cannot out-transfuse an autoantibody. Transfused platelets wear the same target and die in hours. No prophylactic transfusion for a low count alone — the opposite of chemo-induced thrombocytopenia, where <10 gets transfused. The single exception: active critical bleeding, where you transfuse and do not postpone.
9In critical bleeding: give everything, together. Combination therapy mortality 21.7% vs single intervention 30.2%. The 2026 guideline issued STRONG recommendations on LOW-certainty evidence because the harm is catastrophic. Sequential therapy is how you lose the patient politely.
10Do NOT use rFVIIa. Do NOT use plasmapheresis. The 2026 guideline advises against rFVIIa (thrombosis); ICR 2019 lists both as not recommended. They survive in older teaching and in "in extremis" folklore. Plasmapheresis is the treatment for TTP — reaching for it usually means someone confused the two diseases.
11Eltrombopag fails because of breakfast. Polyvalent cations — calcium, iron, magnesium, antacids, milk — chelate it. 2 hours before / 4 hours after. Ask HOW they take it before you escalate the dose. And avatrombopag is the exact opposite: take it WITH food.
12Rilzabrutinib + PPI = a switched-off drug. pH-dependent solubility; avoid PPIs entirely. A very real trap, because half these patients are on a PPI for their steroids.
13Screen HBsAg AND anti-HBc before rituximab. Anti-HBc catches the resolved/occult carrier who is HBsAg-negative and can still fatally reactivate — up to 24 months later. Checking only HBsAg is the classic, potentially fatal miss.
14Defer splenectomy ≥12 months, and vaccinate ≥14 days before — and BEFORE rituximab. Persistent ITP still remits spontaneously, and you cannot un-remove a spleen. Rituximab abolishes the vaccine response, so sequencing them backwards leaves you splenectomising an unvaccinated, unresponsive patient.
15Adult ICH is 1.4–2.2%, not "<1%." The "<1%" everyone quotes is the paediatric figure (0.1–0.4%). And ITP does not enlarge the spleen — a palpable spleen means you are looking at a different disease.
If you remember one idea from this entire guide: "ITP is a syndrome rather than a unique pathology. Different pathological pathways lead to a common feature — thrombocytopenia." The antibody, the spleen, the liver, the complement, the T cells and the sabotaged marrow are six different diseases wearing one name. That is why response is unpredictable, why ~15% have no detectable antibody at all, and why the rational move in a refractory patient is not a bigger dose — it is a different mechanism.
