Guidelines — and what each one does NOT cover

Guideline status as of July 2026 — verifiedASH 2019 and ICR 2019 remain the current comprehensive guidelines. There is no successor to ICR 2019 of any kind. ASH's own 2022 evidence re-review (published 2024) concluded that new evidence was insufficient to justify a full revision, and recommended only a focused update limited to adult second-line therapy. That focused update went out for public comment 12 Nov – 12 Dec 2025 and, as of July 2026, is still listed by ASH as "In development" — it is not finalised, and when it lands it will augment rather than replace the 2019 guideline. The only finalised new document is the narrow 2026 emergency critical-bleeding guideline.
  • ASH 2019 — Neunert C, Terrell DR, Arnold DM, et al. American Society of Hematology 2019 guidelines for immune thrombocytopenia. Blood Adv. 2019;3(23):3829–3866. PMID 31794604 · PMC full text · Blood Advances
    ⚠️ Scope limits, verbatim: it does "not address emergency management of ITP, pregnancy, or treatments that were introduced after 2017." Its evidence review cut off May 2017 — so fostamatinib, avatrombopag and rilzabrutinib are absent, and its adult recommendations cover only corticosteroids, TPO-RA, rituximab and splenectomy. Its IVIG/anti-D recommendations are PAEDIATRIC.
  • ICR 2019 (International Consensus Report) — Provan D, Arnold DM, Bussel JB, et al. Updated international consensus report on the investigation and management of primary immune thrombocytopenia. Blood Adv. 2019;3(22):3780–3817. PMID 31770441 · PMC full text
    The operative source for adult IVIG/anti-D, pregnancy, procedural platelet targets and emergency adjuncts.
  • IWG 2009 — Rodeghiero F, Stasi R, Gernsheimer T, et al. Standardization of terminology, definitions and outcome criteria in immune thrombocytopenic purpura of adults and children. Blood. 2009;113(11):2386–2393. Blood · Full-text PDF
    The source of every definition: the phases, "severe," "refractory," the response criteria (CR/R/NR) and the time-to-response table used by every ITP trial.
  • ASH/McMaster 2026 emergency guideline — Chowdhury SR, Sirotich E, Guyatt GH, … Cuker A, Arnold DM. Guideline on the emergency management of critical bleeding in patients with immune thrombocytopenia. Blood Adv. 2026 Feb 4 (online ahead of print). PMID 41637560 · DOI 10.1182/bloodadvances.2025018818 · PubMed · Blood Advances
    The document for critical bleeding — because ASH 2019 explicitly is not. Narrow scope: adults and children, platelets <20 ×109/L, life- or organ-threatening bleeding.
  • ASH 2022 review of the 2019 guidelines — Neunert CE, Arnold DM, Grace RF, et al. Blood Adv. 2024;8(13):3578–3582. PMID 38608258 · Blood Advances
  • IWG 2013 (bleeding assessment / ITP-BAT) — Rodeghiero F, et al. Standardization of bleeding assessment in immune thrombocytopenia. Blood. 2013;121(14):2596–2606. Blood
  • Critical bleeding systematic review — Chowdhury SR, et al. Eur J Haematol. 2025. PMC full text — the source of the 25%/30.6% mortality and combination-vs-single-therapy figures.
  • USPSTF — HIV (A, 2019) · Hepatitis C (B, 2020) · Hepatitis B (B, 2020) · CDC universal HBV screening (MMWR 2023)
  • CDC/ACIP asplenia vaccination — Altered Immunocompetence · Adult Immunization Schedule notes
  • Neuraxial anaesthesia in thrombocytopenia — SOAP Interdisciplinary Consensus Statement (2021) · ISTH SSC Delphi consensus · Systematic review & meta-analysis (2019)
  • StatPearls — Immune Thrombocytopenia · NCBI Bookshelf
📊

Landmark trials — what each one actually proved

TrialYearDesign / NKey resultWhy it matters
LUNA 3
Rilzabrutinib · Kuter, Blood 2025;145(24):2914		 2025 Phase 3, DB, 2:1
N=202 (133/69)
Median ITP 7.7 yr, 4 prior lines		 Durable platelet response 23% vs 0%, P<0.0001. Response ≥50 at 2 consecutive visits 40% vs 9%. Median time to first ≥50: 15 days. Rescue therapy 33% vs 58% (−52%). Grade ≥2 bleeding 4% vs 12% First BTK inhibitor approved for ITP (FDA 29 Aug 2025). A genuinely new mechanism — dual FcγR + BCR blockade without B-cell depletion. Bleeding DECREASED despite BTK inhibition. Use 23%, not the 29% from the later combined DB+OL interim analysis
FIT1 / FIT2
Fostamatinib · Bussel, Am J Hematol 2018;93(7):921		 2018 Two identical phase 3 RCTs, 2:1
N=150 pooled (101/49)
Median ITP 8.5 years		 Stable response 18% (18/101) vs 2% (1/49), P=0.0003. Overall response 43% vs 14%, P=0.0006. Median time to response 15 d. Diarrhoea 31%, hypertension 28% Established the Syk inhibitor class (FDA 2018). Modest but orthogonal — works downstream of FcγR, where nothing else approved acts. Post-dates the ASH 2019 evidence cutoff, so no guideline places it
RAISE
Eltrombopag · Cheng, Lancet 2011;377(9763):393		 2011 Phase 3, DB, ~2:1, 6 months
N=197 (135/62)
Baseline platelets <30		 OR of response 8.2 (99% CI 3.59–18.73), P<0.0001. Responded at least once 79% vs 28%. Rescue therapy 18% vs 40%. Serious bleeding <1% vs 7%. Reduced concomitant ITP meds 59% vs 32% Pivotal trial for eltrombopag. A very large effect size, and it moved the outcomes that matter — less bleeding, less rescue, less background medication, not just a prettier number
Romiplostim pivotal
Kuter, Lancet 2008;371(9610):395		 2008 Two parallel DB RCTs, 2:1, 24 wk
N=63 splenectomised (42/21)
N=62 non-splenectomised (41/21)		 Durable response — splenectomised 16/42 (38%) vs 0/21, P=0.0013; non-splenectomised 25/41 (61%) vs 1/21 (5%), P<0.0001. Overall response 79% and 88%. 87% reduced/discontinued concurrent ITP therapy vs 38% Pivotal for romiplostim (FDA 2008) — the first TPO-RA to phase 3. Worked regardless of splenectomy status, which anti-D and (mechanistically) splenectomy-dependent strategies cannot claim. Note: the "splenectomy rate 9% vs 36%" figure belongs to Kuter's 2010 NEJM standard-of-care trial, not this one
EXTEND
Eltrombopag long-term · Wong, Blood 2017;130(23):2527		 2017 Open-label extension, single-arm
N=302
Median exposure 2.37 yr (up to 8.76 yr)		 85.8% achieved platelets ≥50 at least once; 52% had continuous response ≥25 weeks. Bleeding fell 57% → 16% at 1 yr. Thromboembolic events 6%, hepatobiliary AEs 15% — NEITHER increased with treatment beyond 1 year The durability and long-term safety answer RAISE could not give. Critically, it defused the fear that TPO-RA thrombotic/hepatic risk accumulates with time — it does not. Published in Blood, not Am J Hematol (that's the separate HRQoL sub-study)
Wei et al
HD-dexamethasone vs prednisone · Blood 2016;127(3):296		 2016 Multicentre RCT
N=192 newly diagnosed, treatment-naive
DXM 40 mg ×4 d vs pred 1 mg/kg ×4 wk		 Initial response 82.1% vs 67.4%, P=0.044; CR 50.5% vs 26.8%, P=0.001; median time to response 3 d vs 6 d, P<0.001. BUT sustained response at 6 months 40.0% vs 41.2%, P=0.884 — NO DIFFERENCE The trial that settles the first-line steroid question honestly. Dexamethasone buys speed, tolerability and ~4 days of steroid instead of 4+ weeks — not durability. Both arms land in the same place at 6 months. Reproduced by Mazzucconi, Blood Adv 2024 (initial 93.9% vs 78.6%; final 59.0% vs 60.5%, NS)
FLIGHT
MMF first-line · Bradbury, NEJM 2021;385(10):885		 2021 Multicentre, open-label RCT, 1:1 (UK)
N=120 (59 MMF+steroid / 61 steroid alone)
Mean baseline platelets 7 ×109/L		 Treatment failure 22% (13/59) vs 44% (27/61), HR 0.41, P=0.008; response (platelets >100) 91.5% vs 63.9%, P<0.001. No difference in bleeding, rescue therapy or infection. BUT the MMF group reported WORSE quality of life — physical function and fatigue (the decrement was domain-specific; mental health and bleeding-concern scores did not differ) The trial that refuses to be simple. Adding MMF up front halves treatment failure — and makes patients feel worse. A reminder that the platelet count is a surrogate and the patient is the endpoint. Not standard first-line practice
Avatrombopag phase 3
Jurczak, Br J Haematol 2018;183(3):479		 2018 Phase 3, DB, placebo-controlled, 2:1
N=49 (32 avatrombopag / 17 placebo)
Chronic ITP ≥12 mo, platelets <30		 Primary endpoint = cumulative weeks with platelets ≥50 without rescue over 6 months: median 12.4 vs 0.0 weeks, P<0.0001. Response at day 8 65.6% vs 0%. Durable response 34.4% vs 0%, P=0.009. 3/32 (9.4%) thromboembolic events (one DVT, one PE, one CVA) — in a very small N Basis for FDA approval for chronic ITP (June 2019). The smallest evidence base of the three TPO-RAs — the honest cost of its convenience advantages (with food, no cation rule, no LFT monitoring, no boxed warning). Post-dates the ASH 2019 cutoff, so no guideline places it
STOPAGO
TPO-RA discontinuation · Guillet, Blood 2023;141(23):2867
Long-term: Cottu, Blood 2025;145(2):244		 2023
2025		 Prospective, multicentre (20 French centres), single-arm
N=48 adults with an established stable response on a TPO-RA ≥1 yr
Standardised stepwise taper		 Sustained response off treatment (SROT): 56.3% at week 24; 52.1% at week 52. After ≥4 more years of follow-up: SROT 47.9% (23/48), sustained COMPLETE response 39.6% (19/48) The evidence that "TPO-RAs are not curative" is only half true. Roughly half of chronic ITP patients with an established complete response can stop the drug and stay stable for 4+ years. A direct argument against indefinite, default-continued therapy. The Blood commentary on this ("STOP & GO", Connell, 2025;145(2):151) is an editorial, not a trial
TAPER
Eltrombopag early 2nd-line · Cooper, Am J Hematol 2024;99(1):57		 2024 Phase 2, prospective, open-label, single-arm
N=105, ITP relapsed/refractory after first-line steroids		 Sustained remission off treatment through month 12: 30.5% (32/105) vs a prespecified null of 15%, P<0.0001. Median SRoT duration ~22 months in those followed to month 24 Tests whether giving a TPO-RA EARLY (straight after steroid failure, before rituximab/splenectomy) can buy a drug-free remission rather than indefinite dependence. Single-arm — no control. Note: no randomised trial of TPO-RA discontinuation exists; every SROT study is single-arm or observational
ADVANCE IV
Efgartigimod (FcRn) · Broome, Lancet 2023;402(10413):1648		 2023 Phase 3, DB, placebo-controlled, 2:1
N=131; primary population = chronic ITP (78/40)		 Sustained platelet response 22% (17/78) vs 5% (2/40), P=0.032. Median weeks of disease control 2.0 vs 0.0 (P=0.0009). BUT the subcutaneous ADVANCE SC trial MISSED its primary endpoint: 13.7% vs 16.2%, P=0.51 The FcRn-antagonist mechanism — block IgG recycling, accelerate catabolism of the pathogenic autoantibody. ⚠️ NOT FDA-approved for ITP as of July 2026 — approved for ITP only in Japan (March 2024). The confirmatory ADVANCE-NEXT trial is ongoing; argenx's own topline guidance has slipped twice (2H2026 → Q4 2026 → H1 2027). Treat as investigational in the US
Kojouri et al
Splenectomy · Blood 2004;104(9):2623		 2004 Systematic review
135 case series, 1966–2004		 Complete response in 1731/2623 (66%) of adults; CR rates did not correlate with duration of follow-up. Mortality 1.0% open vs 0.2% laparoscopic; complications 12.9% vs 9.6% The evidence that splenectomy is genuinely durable — responses did not decay with follow-up. Still the most effective long-term therapy in ITP, and the reason IWG 2009 anchored "refractory" to it. Also established laparoscopic as the preferred technique
Scaradavou et al
Anti-D · Blood 1997;89(8):2689		 1997 Cohort, n=272 ~72% response in D-positive patients; mean platelet increase ~76,000/µL; response >21 days in 50% of responders. ~62% had a haemoglobin decrease by day 7. "Splenectomised patients: minimal or no response" Mechanistic proof that anti-D requires an intact spleen — the drug works by feeding the splenic macrophages a decoy. Remove the spleen and there is nothing to blockade. Also quantifies the haemolysis that is the price of the mechanism
McMaster ITP Registry
Arnold et al		 2017 Prospective adjudicated registry
n=305		 Misdiagnosis rate 15.1%; 12.2% of "primary ITP" reclassified — MDS the commonest (7). Misdiagnosed patients had milder counts (median 43 vs 15). Bleeding: 14.9% none, 42.8% skin/mouth, 7.1% GI, 4.1% GU, 2.2% ICH The hard number behind "ITP is a diagnosis of exclusion." Nearly 1 in 7 was wrong — and the counterintuitive tell is that the MILDER the thrombocytopenia, the more suspicious you should be
Hato et al
Bleeding risk · Blood Adv 2020;4(8):1648		 2020 Nationwide cohort (Japan)
n=19,415 adults		 ICH incidence 1.1%. Independent risk factors for ICH: age ≥60 (OR 3.09, 95% CI 2.13–4.47, P<0.001), platelet <10 (OR 2.96), haematuria (OR 1.56) The best age-stratified ICH data available. Quantifies what IWG 2009 asserted — bleeding risk rises with age. Contested nuance: Crickx (Clin Interv Aging 2023) found age lost significance after adjusting for anticoagulant exposure — the confounder may be the drugs, not the years
PLASMIC derivation
Bendapudi, Lancet Haematol 2017;4(4):e157		 2017 Derivation + internal + external validation cohorts 7-point score. Severe ADAMTS13 deficiency by band: 0–4 = 0–4%; 5 = 5–24%; 6–7 = 62–82%. C statistic 0.91–0.96 The bedside tool that separates ITP from the TTP that will kill your patient while you write for prednisone. Reimplemented live in the Clinic tab
Cuker 4Ts meta-analysis
Blood 2012;120(20):4160		 2012 Systematic review & meta-analysis
13 studies, n=3068		 NPV of a low-probability 4Ts score = 0.998 (95% CI 0.970–1.000). PPV intermediate 0.14, high 0.64 A low 4Ts score reliably excludes HIT — the other can't-miss ITP mimic, and the one where the treatment is backwards (anticoagulate, don't transfuse). Reimplemented live in the Clinic tab
PATCH
Baharoglu, Lancet 2016		 2016 Multicentre RCT, open-label, masked endpoint, 1:1
N=190 (97 transfusion / 93 standard care)
Spontaneous supratentorial ICH on antiplatelet therapy		 Platelet transfusion made outcomes WORSE: adjusted common OR for death or dependence at 3 months 2.05 (95% CI 1.18–3.56), P=0.0114. Poor outcome 72% vs 56%. Serious adverse events 42% vs 29%. And haematoma growth did NOT differ (2.01 vs 1.16 mL, P=0.81) — undercutting the whole hypothesised mechanism Included as a deliberate contrast — do NOT generalise it to ITP. PATCH patients had normal counts and inhibited platelets; the ITP patient has almost no platelets at all. The 2026 guideline recommends transfusion in ITP critical bleeding regardless

Key mechanism & background reading

  • Pathogenesis review — Immune Thrombocytopenia: Recent Advances in Pathogenesis and Treatments. PMC8171374 — source of the antibody frequencies, desialylation/Ashwell–Morell data, complement and T-cell biology, and the "ITP is a syndrome" framing
  • Kuter DJ — Thrombopoietin and Platelet Production in Chronic Immune Thrombocytopenia. PMC2789970
  • Emmons RV et al — the classic proof that TPO is high in megakaryocyte deficiency and low in increased destruction. PubMed
  • Cines DB, Bussel JB, Liebman HA, Luning Prak ET — The ITP syndrome: pathogenic and clinical diversity. Blood 2009. PMC2710913
  • Immune attack on megakaryocytes in ITP · PMC10960061
  • I-WISh (ITP World Impact Survey) — the fatigue/QoL data. PMC7898815
  • Older adults and ITP — Crickx E, et al. Clin Interv Aging 2023;18:115–130. PMC9885884
  • TPO-RA tapering / sustained remission off treatment (SROT) — STOPAGO (Guillet, Blood 2023) · STOPAGO long-term follow-up (Cottu, Blood 2025) · "STOP & GO" editorial (Connell, Blood 2025;145(2):151) — a commentary on STOPAGO, not a trial · TAPER (Cooper, Am J Hematol 2024) · Ten-step tapering review · RAND/UCLA Delphi consensus on tapering
  • Efgartigimod in ITP — ADVANCE IV (Broome, Lancet 2023) · ADVANCE SC — negative (Miyakawa, Am J Hematol 2026) · ADVANCE-NEXT (ongoing, NCT06544499). Not FDA-approved for ITP as of July 2026; approved for ITP in Japan only
  • Anti-D boxed warning background — Despotovic et al. PMC3427798
  • Pseudothrombocytopenia · PMC5164902 · OHSU platelet-clumping protocol

A note on how this guide handles uncertaintyWhere a dose, threshold or figure could not be verified against a primary source, this guide says so explicitly rather than presenting a confident number. You will find those admissions on: the VTE-prophylaxis threshold, the safe-to-discharge count, the ICU downgrade threshold, the adult romiplostim weight-reassessment interval, MMF/dapsone/cyclophosphamide ITP dosing, wet purpura's predictive value, the ITP-specific portal-vein-thrombosis incidence, and per-sign presentation frequencies. Those gaps are real features of the evidence base, not omissions. Medicine's confident tone often outruns its citations; this guide tries not to.
